WHY: Creates hidden ordering dependency (requires Contextual before Logger in pluginsintegration.go:160-161); standalone/reordered use silently logs without plugin identity. HOW: Keep explicit fallback from req.PluginContext/tracing when ctx has no attributes, or document/enforce ordering.

issues.descricao: Claims the metrics middleware now fails the request when the plugin is not in the registry.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: QueryData (and CallResource:161) abort the plugin call and return ErrPluginNotRegistered when instrumentPluginRequestSize/pluginTarget lookup fails. WHY: A best-effort observability lookup failure becomes a request failure, blocking the real plugin call that might have returned its own error. HOW: Log the target-lookup failure and continue to instrumentPluginRequest/next call instead of returning early.

Best-effort metrics now fails the request: QueryData (and CallResource/CheckHealth/CollectMetrics via the same helpers) returns ErrPluginNotRegistered from pluginTarget/instrumentPluginRequestSize without calling next when the plugin is missing from the registry. Callers lose the previous contract that instrumentation never refuses the request. Fix: do not propagate registry miss as request error — default target to unknown/skip observation and always invoke next.

sugestoes.texto: The asynchronous legacy write inherits cancellation from the HTTP request context despite its new ten-second timeout. Once the response completes, request cancellation can abort the legacy operation or cause it to start with an already-cancelled context, leaving successful unified writes unreplicated; the same defect affects Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. Derive the bounded background context from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) so namespace and identity values survive without inheriting request cancellation.

Legacy.Update now receives the original objInfo rather than a wrapper containing the object committed to unified storage. playlist legacyStorage.Update calls objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old) on its own legacy object, so a patch is recalculated against potentially stale legacy state and can fail or persist a different result from the successful unified update. Restore updateWrapper with updated: res for the legacy call.

Successful Delete records the resource name in the histogram's kind label instead of options.Kind. metrics.go passes this value directly into the global HistogramVec, retaining a separate histogram for every distinct deleted object name and causing memory and exported-series growth as resources churn. Pass options.Kind consistently with the error path and other operations.

The successful Update test only checks the returned unified-store object, while both backends share the same mock and identical Update expectations. There is no condition that waits for and verifies the legacy write. Deleting the Legacy.Update goroutine entirely would still pass this test; the Create test has the same blind spot. Use separate backend mocks and a completion signal for the legacy invocation, then verify its arguments and call count after completion so these tests actually distinguish mode 3 from storage-only writes.

This case says creation happens only in the unified store, but it sets up Legacy.Create as well, and Mode3.Create explicitly launches that legacy write after Storage.Create succeeds. The test output therefore describes the opposite of the dual-write behavior being exercised; name it as a write to both stores.

The case description says listing is not implemented, but this PR implements List by delegating to Storage.List. This case merely returns errors.New("error") from that mock and checks propagation; it does not simulate or assert an unimplemented-operation error. Rename it to describe a unified-store listing failure so test reports do not incorrectly imply Mode3 lacks List support.

The legacy write now runs after the method returns, but its timeout still inherits the request context. When the HTTP handler finishes, that context is canceled; a legacy call scheduled afterward (or still doing database work) therefore fails despite a successful unified write. This affects Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection and can systematically leave the stores inconsistent. Detach request cancellation while preserving context values before starting the bounded background work, or complete the write before returning.

Returning before the legacy update finishes removes ordering even for sequential client requests. Update A can commit to unified storage and return, then update B commits and its legacy goroutine runs first; A's delayed legacy goroutine can subsequently overwrite B (or B can fail a version check), leaving legacy storage with A while unified storage contains B. Create followed by Delete can similarly run legacy Delete before legacy Create and resurrect a deleted object. Preserve commit ordering for background writes per resource, or keep these writes synchronous.

This branch follows Storage.Create, but records a legacy duration even though no legacy call occurs. The same copy-paste error occurs in the Storage.Update error branch at line 129. Consequently storage failures disappear from storage metrics and falsely inflate legacy failures and timings. Use recordStorageDuration in both storage error branches.

Every other duration emission, including this method's error branch and legacy call, passes options.Kind in this position. Passing name on success splits success and failure measurements across different kind values and creates a separate metric series for each deleted object. Pass options.Kind consistently.

This timing surrounds Legacy.DeleteCollection, but emits through recordStorageDuration. A successful collection deletion therefore emits two storage measurements and no legacy measurement; a legacy failure is also incorrectly reported as a storage failure. Record this call with recordLegacyDuration.

The preceding line enriches log with name, kind and method, but the context receives d.Log instead. Storage and legacy code retrieving the context logger therefore lose those operation fields, unlike the other methods. Install log in the context.

Create now returns before Legacy.Create completes, but the goroutine derives its timeout from the original request context. HTTP request contexts are canceled when the handler returns, so a successful primary write can immediately cancel its legacy mirror, leaving the stores inconsistent. The same mismatch affects Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. Detach cancellation while preserving request values (for example with context.WithoutCancel(ctx)) before applying the bounded timeout, or retain synchronous completion.

Previously Legacy.Update received an updateWrapper containing the object returned by Storage.Update. Passing the original objInfo instead makes the legacy consumer invoke UpdatedObject against its own old object. For patches or transforms, especially when legacy data is stale, this can produce a different object (or fail on a patch precondition) despite the primary update succeeding. Preserve the wrapper with updated: res so the legacy write mirrors the committed primary result rather than independently evaluating the update.

issues.descricao: Delete puts the base d.Log instead of the enriched per-call logger into the context, so downstream logs lose name/kind/method fields.
issues.textoGolden: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

comentarios.texto: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` installs the mode-level logger instead of the request-scoped `log` built on line 96 (which carries name, kind and method) — a copy/paste error, as every other method in this file passes the composed `log`. Storage.Delete and the legacy delete goroutine therefore log without the per-request fields this PR is adding (and without the metrics method/kind context).
ctx is built with klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of the enriched `log`. The delete logs then lose the name, kind and method values. Use `log`.
The Delete context uses d.Log rather than the per-call log. This is a logging-context inconsistency (not a data leak); use the per-call logger for consistency.

issues.descricao: The legacy DeleteCollection goroutine records its duration with recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, misattributing legacy latency and errors to the storage metric.
issues.textoGolden: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

comentarios.texto: The legacy DeleteCollection duration and error status are recorded in the unified-storage histogram. Every successful unified deletion therefore produces a second storage observation for a different backend, while legacy deletion failures are attributed to unified storage and no legacy observation is emitted. Call recordLegacyDuration here instead.

The timed call is d.Legacy.DeleteCollection, but its measurement is emitted using recordStorageDuration. Use recordLegacyDuration; otherwise storage receives two measurements for a successful collection deletion and legacy receives none, and legacy failures appear as storage failures.
The legacy DeleteCollection duration is recorded with recordStorageDuration, so legacy latency and errors are attributed to storage. Use recordLegacyDuration.

issues.descricao: Delete's success path records the storage metric with the object name in the kind label instead of options.Kind, creating per-object series and inconsistent labels.
issues.textoGolden: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

comentarios.texto: The Delete success-path metric passes `name` where every other call site in this file (lines 48, 103, 113, 156, 159) passes options.Kind in the kind/name argument slot. The storage-success sample for Delete is thus labelled with the object name instead of the resource kind, breaking label consistency with the other operations and with the error sample emitted at line 103. Use options.Kind here (or insert name consistently everywhere, matching the metric's label semantics).
recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) at line 106 passes the object name in the kind label slot.

recordStorageDuration is called with the object `name` as the `kind` label: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`. Every other storage call site passes `options.Kind` (lines 73, 89, 103, 156, 159). This injects a per-object value into the kind label, corrupting the metric and giving it unbounded cardinality (one series per object name), which grows memory on every delete. Should be `options.Kind`.

issues.descricao: On storage Create/Update failure the duration is recorded with recordLegacyDuration, attributing unified-store errors to the legacy metric.

comentarios.texto: On a Storage.Create failure the code records the error with recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) — the failing subsystem is Storage, not Legacy, and it passes the storage start time. This records storage failures under the legacy metric, corrupting the dual-writer error dashboards (and contradicts the success path on line 48 which uses recordStorageDuration). Use d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

On a Storage.Update failure the code records the error with recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage), attributing a storage failure and its storage duration to the legacy metric. This is inconsistent with the success path on line 132 (recordStorageDuration) and with mode1's semantics. Use d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

The async goroutine performing the LEGACY DeleteCollection measures it with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). Every other legacy write in this file uses recordLegacyDuration (lines 56, 113, 140); recording it under the storage metric reports legacy latency/errors as storage latency/errors. Use d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy).

issues.descricao: Mode 3 legacy writes now run in background goroutines derived from the request context, which is cancelled when the request completes, so legacy writes can be cancelled and legacy storage falls out of sync.

comentarios.texto: The async legacy write goroutine derives its context from the request-scoped `ctx` (context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)). The apiserver cancels that context as soon as the HTTP handler returns — which is immediately after Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection return — so the goroutine's Legacy.Create can be canceled before completing, silently dropping the legacy write that this mode exists to guarantee. The same applies to the goroutines at lines 108-114, 134-141 and 161-167. Detach the async context from request cancellation (e.g. derive from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) / context.Background()) before applying the timeout.

The legacy write in Mode 3 became fire-and-forget, changing the contract callers relied on: previously Create (and, identically, Update/Delete/DeleteCollection) returned only after the LegacyStorage call had been made in-request; now it returns immediately and the write runs in a detached goroutine. Worse, the goroutine builds its context from the request-scoped `ctx` (line 51: `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`), which the API server cancels as soon as the handler returns/flushes the response — so the legacy write and its 10s timeout will typically be cancelled outright and the legacy store silently stops being updated, which is precisely what the new mode-3 integration cases assume still happens. Any detached work must be given a context not tied to the request lifetime (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a server-lifetime context), and consumers that depended on the synchronous legacy write need to be updated.

The asynchronous legacy write derives its timeout context from the request context, which is canceled when the HTTP request finishes. Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection return before this work completes, so their legacy database operations can be canceled immediately instead of receiving the intended ten-second window. Derive the bounded background context from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) to retain request values without inheriting request cancellation.

issues.descricao: Legacy.Update now receives the original objInfo instead of a wrapper carrying the object stored in unified storage, so legacy recomputes the update and can diverge.

comentarios.texto: Legacy.Update receives the original objInfo instead of the object successfully committed to unified storage. The playlist legacy implementation calls objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old) against its own legacy object, so a patch is reapplied to potentially stale state and can persist a different result or fail rather than mirror the unified write. Pass an updateWrapper containing res, as the previous implementation did.

Legacy.Update previously received an updateWrapper containing the object returned by Storage.Update; it now receives the original objInfo. UpdatedObjectInfo can compute an update from the old object supplied by each backend (notably for patches), so evaluating it against a stale legacy object can produce a different result or reject an update that already succeeded in Storage. Preserve the canonical-result contract by passing an updateWrapper with updated: res and upstream: objInfo to the legacy consumer rather than replaying the original update against legacy state.

Legacy.Update now receives the original objInfo rather than the updateWrapper containing the object successfully committed to Storage. UpdatedObjectInfo can represent a patch/transform based on the supplied old object; replaying it against legacy's potentially different old state can persist a different result or fail, even though the authoritative update succeeded. Restore forwarding of the committed result via updateWrapper instead of recomputing the update against legacy state.

issues.descricao: The Mode 3 tests never wait for or assert the asynchronous legacy writes, and legacy and storage share one mock, so removing the legacy calls would not fail them.

comentarios.texto: The legacy half of Mode 3 is never verified, so these tests cannot catch its removal. Mode 3 is documented as writing to BOTH LegacyStorage and Storage, and the implementation performs the legacy write in a detached goroutine (`go func(){ d.Legacy.Create(...) }()`, dualwriter_mode3.go lines 50-57, and likewise at 108-114, 134-141, 161-167). Each test registers legacy expectations (`setupLegacyFn`, e.g. lines 30-32 and 40-42) but never calls `m.AssertExpectations(t)`, `AssertCalled` or `AssertNumberOfCalls`, and never waits for or observes the goroutine — no channel, no polling. Additionally `legacyStoreMock{m, l}` and `storageMock{m, s}` (lines 53-54, and the same pair in every other test function) share one `*mock.Mock`, so even a count assertion could not distinguish a legacy call from a storage call. Deleting every `d.Legacy.*` call from the implementation leaves all six tests passing, which is exactly the regression the names — and the Mode 3 contract — claim to cover.

The successful Create test never verifies the legacy write. Configuring m.On("Create", ...) does not require that expectation to be consumed, and these assertions only inspect the object returned by Storage.Create. Deleting the entire legacy-create goroutine would still pass this test. Use distinct storage and legacy mocks and synchronize on the legacy call, then assert that it completed with the intended object.

The successful Update case configures a legacy Update expectation but returns after checking only the unified-store result. It neither waits for the asynchronous legacy update nor verifies its expectation, so removing the legacy-update goroutine entirely still passes. Add explicit synchronization and verification of the legacy update (ideally with separate mocks), including the object propagated to legacy storage.

issues.descricao: The List error test case is still named 'not implemented' although List is now implemented and the case checks storage error propagation.

comentarios.texto: The test-case name "error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented" still describes the old stub List (which returned nil, nil with a "List not implemented" log). List is now implemented at dualwriter_mode3.go:79 and delegates to Storage.List; the case merely checks that a Storage error is propagated. The name contradicts the code it now exercises — rename it, e.g. "error when listing objects in the unified store fails".

issues.descricao: The Create test case name says 'only in the unified store' although Mode 3 also writes to legacy.

comentarios.texto: The test name says creation happens "only in the unified store", but this case configures a successful Legacy.Create as well, and Mode3.Create launches that legacy write after the unified write succeeds. Rename the case to describe creation in both stores (with the legacy write asynchronous), so test output does not communicate the opposite of the mode-3 write contract.

issues.descricao: Independent per-request goroutines remove ordering between legacy writes to the same resource, so legacy can end up with an older version or a resurrected object.

comentarios.texto: Independent goroutines remove ordering between successful writes to the same resource. For example, Storage commits update A and then update B, but the legacy goroutine for B can finish before A, leaving legacy with A while Storage contains B. Likewise a delete can run before an earlier create and leave a resurrected legacy object. Preserve per-resource commit order for mirroring (including across create/update/delete), rather than launching each write independently.

issues.descricao: The storage-failure Create test registers its failing expectation via setupLegacyFn and only works because legacy and storage share one mock.

comentarios.texto: The 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' case registers the failing Create expectation only through setupLegacyFn. It passes only because legacy and storage share one mock, so the storage Create gets that error by accident. Register the expectation in setupStorageFn and use separate mocks for legacy and storage, so the test really covers a storage failure.

issues.descricao: Claims the Equal/NotEqual assertions in the Mode 3 tests can never fail, though the Equal assertion does fail if Delete stops returning the storage result.

comentarios.texto: Assertions that can never fail. `assert.Equal(t, obj, exampleObj)` compares the value the shared mock was configured to return (`m.On("Delete", ...).Return(exampleObj, false, nil)` at line 202) against that same fixture, so it restates the stub rather than exercising anything; `assert.NotEqual(t, obj, anotherObj)` compares against a different fixture value and is true for every possible return of `dw.Delete`, including `nil`. Either assertion would still pass if the storage call were removed and `nil, 0, nil` returned. The same pair (Equal-against-fixture + NotEqual-against-other-fixture) is repeated at lines 129-130, 183-184, 291-292 and 352-353 in the other tests. Assert something the code actually produces, e.g. that the name/argument passed through to the storage mock matches the input (`us.AssertCalled(t, "Delete", mock.Anything, tt.input, mock.Anything, mock.Anything)`) or assert on the returned error/async flag.

issues.descricao: Claims the legacy-create goroutine races with the caller on a shared obj that can alias the returned object.

comentarios.texto: Goroutine captures mutable obj/options while caller returns object that can alias it; DeepCopy before handing to goroutine to avoid concurrent read/write race.

issues.descricao: Empty comment.

sugestoes.texto: BuildIndex now publishes the index only after building it without preventing another caller from missing the same cache key in the meantime. Concurrent Search calls, or Search racing with handleEvent, can build separate indexes for the same namespace/resource; one replaces the other in the cache, so an event written to the displaced index is lost from subsequent search results. Serialize cache lookup and construction per key, while allowing different keys to build concurrently.

The new initialization log calls TotalDocs after starting the watch-event consumer, but bleveBackend.TotalDocs iterates b.cache without holding cacheMu. A write event for an unindexed resource can cause handleEvent to build and insert an index concurrently with this iteration, causing a data race or a fatal concurrent map iteration/write error during startup. Protect the map iteration in TotalDocs with cacheMu.RLock/RUnlock.

issues.descricao: BuildIndex now locks only the final cache assignment, so concurrent callers for the same uncached key all build the same expensive index in parallel and the last one overwrites the others.
issues.textoGolden: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Removing the function-wide `b.cacheMu.Lock()/defer Unlock()` and keeping only the lock around `b.cache[key]=idx` removes the only thing that serialized GetIndex against an in-flight build. WHY: getOrCreateIndex (resource/search.go:287-307) does GetIndex -> if nil -> build; previously BuildIndex held the write lock for its whole body so a concurrent caller's GetIndex (RLock) blocked until the first build cached the index and then saw it (no second build). Now GetIndex can return nil while a build for the same key is still running, so two requests/watch events build the SAME key concurrently — producing two distinct index instances where the caller holding the non-cached one never observes later writes (stale search results), and, for file-backed indices (size > FileThreshold), two concurrent `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` opening the same on-disk directory. HOW: guard the build per key (e.g. re-check the cache under the write lock after acquiring it, or use a per-key single-flight/lock so only one build runs per NamespacedResource), rather than relying on a global write lock held for the entire body.

The cache mutex was moved to cover only the cache assignment, removing the serialization that previously surrounded the whole BuildIndex. Two concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key can now both construct an index (including `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same on-disk path) and both write `b.cache[key]`; the second overwrites the first, so callers get distinct index instances for one key and writes made through the losing instance are invisible to readers of the cached one (and the file-backed build may collide on the same directory). Keep the build for a given key serialized (e.g. restore the lock around the build, or take a per-key lock) instead of locking only the map write.

Locking only cache publication allows concurrent requests for the same uncached key to build separate indexes and overwrite each other's cache entries. Search and handleEvent both call getOrCreateIndex, whose GetIndex previously blocked behind the build-wide lock; now an event can update one newly built index before another build replaces it, losing that update from subsequent search results and leaving the discarded index open. Serialize builds per NamespacedResource and recheck the cache after acquiring that per-key guard.

issues.descricao: The new startup log calls TotalDocs, which iterates the index cache without a lock, after the event goroutine that can add indexes has started, so a concurrent map read and write can crash the process.
issues.textoGolden: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

comentarios.texto: The newly added `s.search.TotalDocs()` call is unsafe: `bleveBackend.TotalDocs()` (pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:144-150) iterates `b.cache` without holding `cacheMu`, while the bleve.go hunk in this same PR keeps `cacheMu` for the `b.cache[key] = idx` write only. Because search.go:207-213 already started the watch-event goroutine that can call `build` → `BuildIndex` → cache write, line 216 can iterate the map concurrently with that write, causing a `concurrent map iteration and map write` panic or data race. Either guard the `TotalDocs` read with `cacheMu`, or move this call to a point where no build can run concurrently.

The new startup log calls TotalDocs after launching the write-event listener, but bleveBackend.TotalDocs iterates b.cache without cacheMu.RLock. A write event for an unindexed resource can concurrently publish an index through BuildIndex, causing a map iteration/write race and potentially a fatal runtime error during initialization. Protect TotalDocs cache iteration with the same read lock used by GetIndex.

BuildIndex now writes b.cache under Lock while TotalDocs (called from search.init after the watch goroutine starts) ranges over b.cache without any lock. This can cause a concurrent map read/write fatal error. Fix by taking cacheMu.RLock in TotalDocs.

issues.descricao: NewResourceServer returns an error when Init fails without cancelling the server context created earlier.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) and, on error, returns `nil, err` without invoking the `cancel` func created at line 229 and without running any lifecycle cleanup. WHY: Init may have already started long-lived goroutines — searchSupport.init's event-consumption loop uses context.Background() (resource/search.go:202) and initWatcher starts a watcher bound to s.ctx (server.go:752-770) — so if search.init succeeds and initWatcher (or a later step) fails, the constructor discards the server while those goroutines keep running with no way to stop them, leaking the internal context and watcher goroutines. HOW: on the error path call `cancel()` (and any needed lifecycle.Stop) before returning, or defer the cancel until success.

WHAT: NewResourceServer calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously but returns nil,err without calling the cancel created for s.ctx. WHY: Failed startup leaks the server context (and any lifecycle/watch resources partially started by Init), leaving goroutines/channel watches alive. HOW: On Init error call s.cancel() (and lifecycle Stop cleanup) before returning.

issues.descricao: Claims the new postgres t.Skip removes coverage of the storage-server instrumentation test for that backend.

comentarios.texto: The added `t.Skip` for `dbType == "postgres"` makes this the only test covering the storage-server target server's instrumentation HTTP setup stop running entirely for postgres: the early return at lines 36-38 happens before `InitializeModuleServer`/`ms.Run()` and before the `assert.Equal(t, 200, res.StatusCode)` at line 63, so the postgres path could regress (module server not starting, `/metrics` not serving 200, `InitializeModuleServer` erroring) and this test would still pass. Either fix the underlying postgres/Drone failure and keep the assertion running, or add an equivalent postgres-target test that actually brings up the server and checks `/metrics` returns 200, rather than silently removing the coverage.

The new postgres skip bypasses the entire instrumentation-server test for that backend. If the storage-server target stops starting its instrumentation HTTP server on postgres, this case now reports skipped rather than catching the regression, including locally where the comment says it works. Fix the CI-specific failure or isolate its actual environmental prerequisite instead of disabling verification for every postgres run.

issues.descricao: Claims making NewResourceServer call Init changes the constructor contract, blocking on the full index build and failing construction on any index error.

comentarios.texto: `NewResourceServer` now performs initialization itself by calling `s.Init(ctx)`, changing the constructor's contract for every consumer. Previously the constructor returned a usable server and index building was lazy (getOrCreateIndex in search.go builds on first query and surfaces errors per-request). Now construction blocks on the full search-index build (search.init calls GetResourceStats and builds every namespace/resource index) and, on any failure, returns `nil, err` instead of a server — a single index build error now prevents the server from existing at all, rather than degrading to a per-request search error. Additionally, because `Init` is guarded by `sync.Once` (server.go:294), this internal call consumes the once and the context passed by any existing caller to `Init` is no longer the one used for `lifecycle.Init`, `search.init` and `initWatcher` — the constructor's ctx silently wins. Either keep initialization in the caller (revert this call) or make the callers explicitly aware of the new fail-fast, eager-initialization contract.

issues.descricao: Claims starting the watcher after search.init makes writes between the index snapshot and initWatcher never reach the search index.

comentarios.texto: The watcher is now started after search.init, so events written after the index snapshot but before initWatcher runs are never delivered to the index. The index stays permanently stale for those writes. Start the watcher (buffering events) before building the index, or replay events from the index's build resource version after the watcher starts.

sugestoes.texto: GrafanaRuleListItem now supplies only promRule, but AlertRuleMenu still requires rulerRule to render Delete. Consequently, users with delete permission lose the Delete action throughout the new Grafana list. Update the delete menu and handler contract to use the existing identifier/groupIdentifier without requiring a loaded ruler rule.

The new Prometheus-only action props leave AlertRuleMenu's pause item gated by rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule), which is false when rulerRule is absent. Users can no longer pause or resume Grafana rules from the list despite the new ability hook granting Pause. Adapt the pause item to accept the Prometheus rule/identifier and obtain the mutation data when invoked.

RuleActionsButtons now accepts promRule without rule, but its silence drawer still mounts only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true. Clicking the newly enabled Silence notifications item only sets showSilenceDrawer and displays nothing for Grafana list rows. Adapt the drawer to the Prometheus UID or load the ruler rule before mounting it.

useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously checked isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) and marked Update/Delete unsupported for federated Mimir groups. Delegating here drops that group information, and useAllRulerRuleAbilities explicitly sets isFederated=false. Existing consumers of the CombinedRule hook therefore receive mutation abilities for federated rules whenever their datasource permissions allow editing/deleting, instead of the previous immutable result. Preserve the federated-group check in this wrapper or pass the group information into the delegated implementation.

AlertRuleMenu now passes skipToken for every non-Grafana rule and ORs the returned abilities with the ruler abilities. Converting skipToken to undefined does not disable this hook: useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) sets MaybeSupported to AlwaysSupported once loading ends and grants Duplicate based on the user's Grafana rule-create permission. A user with that permission can consequently see Duplicate for a data-source rule even when its own ruler ability is unsupported or denied. Return [false, false] for every requested action when the input is skipToken (and apply the same behavior to the singular hook), while still calling the underlying hooks unconditionally.

issues.descricao: The pause menu item is still gated on a Grafana ruler rule, but the list view now passes only the Prometheus rule, so Pause/Resume disappears for list-view rules even when the user may pause them.

comentarios.texto: The new Prometheus-based pause ability cannot display Pause or Resume for list-view rules because the menu still requires rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) before rendering MenuItemPauseRule. GrafanaRuleListItem now supplies only promRule, so these actions disappear even for editable rules. Adapt the pause menu item to accept the Grafana identifier and Prometheus pause state, or load the ruler rule on demand.

issues.descricao: The Delete menu item still requires a ruler rule, which list-view Grafana rules no longer provide, so users with delete permission lose the Delete action.

comentarios.texto: The new Prometheus-based delete ability is still gated by `canDelete && rulerRule` when rendering the Delete item. Both Grafana list-view paths now omit rulerRule, so users with delete permission lose the Delete action entirely. Render deletion using the available identifier and group identifier instead of requiring the ruler DTO, adapting the callback contract accordingly.

issues.descricao: When the Grafana prom-rule branch is skipped (datasource rules), useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) still reports Duplicate as supported and allowed by Grafana create permission, and AlertRuleMenu ORs it with the ruler ability, so Duplicate appears on cloud rules even when the ruler check denies it.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: canDuplicate ORs ruler ability with grafana ability where grafana path is skipToken=>undefined for cloud rules, and useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) returns Duplicate=[true,true] whenever the user has global Grafana create permission. WHY: Any user with Grafana rule-create gets Duplicate menu item on cloud/Mimir rules even when ruler abilities deny it — incorrect authorization gating. HOW: Return NotSupported for all abilities when rule is skipToken/undefined, or gate grafana branch on prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(promRule) before ORing.

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities returns AlwaysSupported for Duplicate when rule is undefined (skipToken): loading is false from the !rule early-return, so MaybeSupported=true and duplicateSupported=true. ORed in AlertRuleMenu/RuleActionsButtons this leaks Grafana create permission into non-Grafana rules. Gate MaybeSupported/duplicateSupported on rule existence (e.g. NotSupported when !rule).

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities must return NotSupported for all actions when rule is undefined (skipToken). Currently MaybeSupported falls back to AlwaysSupported when !loading, so Duplicate=[true, global-create] is true for a cloud rule passed as skipToken, and AlertRuleMenu/RuleActionsButtons OR-logic then incorrectly enables Duplicate (and Explore). Guard with if (!rule) return all-NotSupported abilities or make MaybeSupported require rule.

issues.descricao: The refactor of useAllAlertRuleAbilities into useAllRulerRuleAbilities drops the isFederatedRuleGroup check (isFederated is hardcoded false), so federated Mimir rules are reported as editable and deletable.

comentarios.texto: useAllAlertRuleAbilities now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated = false. The previous isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) check is gone, so federated Mimir rules are no longer treated as immutable and can show edit and delete abilities. Keep the federation check in this wrapper, or pass the federation state into the shared hook.

Delegating useAllAlertRuleAbilities to useAllRulerRuleAbilities discards the group's federation status and replaces the previous isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) check with a constant false. Legacy RuleActionsButtons consequently enables editing rules in groups with source_tenants, although these groups were explicitly immutable before this change. Preserve the CombinedRule federation check in the wrapper or pass federation status into the delegated ability calculation.

Preserve the federated-group immutability check when delegating this CombinedRule hook. Previously useAllAlertRuleAbilities inspected rule.group with isFederatedRuleGroup and disabled modification/removal for federated rules. The replacement delegates to a hook that hardcodes isFederated=false and receives no group information. Existing useAlertRuleAbility/useAlertRuleAbilities consumers therefore now receive supported update/delete abilities for federated rules when datasource permissions allow them, exposing operations that the previous contract explicitly prohibited. Pass the federation state through or retain that restriction in this wrapper.

issues.descricao: The Grafana prom-rule abilities gate Pause, Restore, Export and DeletePermanently on alertingRule(rule) while the comment claims it checks Grafana-managed rules, so Grafana recording rules lose these actions in the list view.

comentarios.texto: The comment says all GrafanaPromRuleDTO rules are Grafana-managed, but the variable it describes is `isAlertingRule`. That variable is true only for alerting rules and false for Grafana recording rules. Fix the comment, or rename the variable, so it says the check is for alerting rules. As written, readers will expect Pause, Export and Silence to be enabled for recording rules.

The comment says all GrafanaPromRuleDTO rules are Grafana-managed, but the check used is alertingRule(rule), which is false for recording rules. Pause, Restore, ModifyExport and DeletePermanently are therefore wrongly disabled for Grafana recording rules, where the old isGrafanaManagedAlertRule check allowed them. Use prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(rule) for these abilities, and keep alertingRule only for Silence.

issues.descricao: The comment claims GrafanaPromRuleDTO abilities have no loading state, but the next line makes support depend on the folder loading flag.

comentarios.texto: The comment says there is no loading state, but the next line is `loading ? NotSupported : AlwaysSupported`. `loading` comes from the folder fetch. Update the comment to say that support depends on the folder loading state.

issues.descricao: The Grafana branch of the filtered rule list renders GrafanaRuleListItem without a key prop, so React reconciles the streaming list by index and warns about missing keys.
issues.textoGolden: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The grafana branch of the filtered list renders <GrafanaRuleListItem .../> without a `key` prop, dropping the `key={key}` that the replaced <GrafanaRuleLoader key={key} .../> had. WHY: `rules.map` renders a dynamic list keyed by getRuleKey/hashRule; without a key React logs duplicate-key warnings and reconciles rows by index, so as the async rule stream updates/reorders the wrong rule row can be reused/mutated (stale state, swapped actions). HOW: add `key={key}` (the value is already destructured on line 152) to the <GrafanaRuleListItem> element.

WHAT: Grafana branch of FilterViewResults renders GrafanaRuleListItem without key={key} while datasource and unknown branches pass key. WHY: Breaks React list reconciliation — wrong item reuse, stale actions/state and console key warnings for every Grafana hit. HOW: Add key={key} to the GrafanaRuleListItem element.

issues.descricao: The test named 'should render More button with action menu options' only checks the More button exists, never the menu options.

comentarios.texto: The test 'should render More button with action menu options' only checks that the More button exists. It finds the button by name 'More', so the aria-label and text assertions are tautological. It would pass even if the menu had no actions or the abilities were broken. Click the button and assert the expected menu items, or rename the test to match what it checks.

Test named 'should render More button with action menu options' never verifies any action menu option: the body only asserts the More button exists and has aria-label/text 'More'. It would still pass if the dropdown were rendered empty (Silence/Duplicate/Copy link/Export all missing), i.e. the behaviour the name promises is not covered. Either open the menu and assert the menu items, or rename the test to reflect that it only checks the trigger button's rendering/accessibility.

Test named 'should render More button with action menu options' never opens the menu nor asserts menu items — it only checks More button presence/aria/text. Click More and assert expected menuitems (or rename to 'should render More button') so it fails if menu actions break.

issues.descricao: GrafanaGroupLoader's JSDoc still says it loads from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints after the ruler query was removed.

comentarios.texto: The JSDoc for GrafanaGroupLoader still says "Loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints." but this PR removed the ruler API query entirely — the component now only calls useGetGrafanaGroupsQuery (Prometheus). The documentation describes a data source the function no longer consumes; update it to state only the Prometheus endpoint is loaded (and the same stale "Ruler response" reference in the expectedRulesCount prop doc at lines 18–19 should be corrected).

issues.descricao: For list-view Grafana rules RuleActionsButtons gets only promRule, so the Silence menu item is shown but the silence drawer, still gated on a ruler alerting rule, never renders and clicking Silence does nothing.
issues.textoGolden: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.

comentarios.texto: Passing only promRule enables the Silence notifications menu item but leaves RuleActionsButtons.V2 unable to render its silence drawer, which is guarded by rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule). Clicking Silence only updates showSilenceDrawer and displays nothing because rule is undefined. Update the drawer to accept a rule UID—the inspected SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer only needs grafana_alert.uid—and allow the Prometheus alerting-rule path to render it.

The new list item passes only promRule to RuleActionsButtons, but that component renders SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer only under `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer`. With rule undefined, clicking the newly enabled 'Silence notifications' action only sets state and never opens a drawer. Adapt the silence rendering path to load/use the rule by its Prometheus identifier before switching this caller to promRule-only.

WHAT: getEditableIdentifier now enables a prom-only path (Grafana uid identifier with rulerRule undefined) but the silence drawer still renders only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true. WHY: In the list view Silence menu item can be shown via grafana abilities, clicking it sets showSilenceDrawer but the drawer never mounts, so Silence silently does nothing. HOW: Gate the drawer on promRule as well or provide a prom-based silence drawer.

issues.descricao: Claims provisioned status now comes from promRule.provenance, which the Prometheus response might omit, making provisioned rules editable.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: isProvisioned derived from promRule.provenance (new optional field) instead of ruler grafana_alert.provenance. WHY: If the Prometheus groups response omits provenance, provisioned rules render as non-provisioned and abilities (isProvisionedPromRule) fail open to editable/removable. HOW: Ensure Prometheus API populates provenance or fall back to ruler/folder metadata for the provisioned check.

issues.descricao: Claims the promRule prop typed as Rule makes the Grafana prom-rule type guard return false for the GrafanaPromRuleDTO passed by GrafanaRuleListItem.

comentarios.texto: The `promRule` prop is declared as `Rule` (the combined-rule type from app/types/unified-alerting, the same type used for `useRulePluginLinkExtension`), but the body consumes it as a `GrafanaPromRuleDTO`: it feeds it to `prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(promRule) ? promRule : skipToken` -> `useGrafanaPromRuleAbility(rule: GrafanaPromRuleDTO | SkipToken, …)` and to `isProvisionedPromRule(promRule: PromRuleDTO)`. The new producer GrafanaRuleListItem.tsx passes a raw GrafanaPromRuleDTO into this `Rule`-typed slot. Because `Rule` is not a prom-rule DTO, the type guard returns false for combined-rule callers (e.g. the RulesTable path) so the Grafana abilities resolve to NotSupported and the new menu entries are silently hidden, while the list-view caller only appears to work by passing a differently-typed object. Align the prop type with what the hooks/guards require (GrafanaPromRuleDTO) on the side the caller must satisfy, and update GrafanaRuleListItem accordingly.

sugestoes.texto: The new grant-context extraction records client_credentials tokens as unknown because ClientCredentialsGrantType.process generates tokens directly without setting Constants.GRANT_TYPE or calling createTokenResponse. Consequently service-account access tokens receive the na grant shortcut even though the cc factory is registered, so decoding cannot recover their grant type. Set Constants.GRANT_TYPE from context.getGrantType() in ClientCredentialsGrantType before generateAccessToken(), as done for the password grant.

isAccessTokenId checks substring(3, 5) and rejects equality, although the encoder stores the grant shortcut at indices 4 and 5. The code, refresh, device and CIBA event assertions therefore accept an incorrect grant shortcut whenever the suffix is a UUID, masking regressions in the new metadata. Require a six-character prefix and reject when substring(4, 6) does not equal the expected shortcut.

The encoder puts the grant shortcut at indices 4–5, but this matcher reads indices 3–4 and returns false on equality rather than inequality. For example, onrtac:<UUID> passes when the expected grant is rt, so these event assertions do not detect tokens issued with the wrong grant. Check the prefix length and compare substring(4, 6), rejecting a mismatch.

The new extension contract tells implementers to return a three-letter shortcut, but DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider requires a six-character context and decodes the grant from substring(4, 6), leaving exactly two characters. An extension following this documentation produces token IDs that the decoder rejects. Document the mandatory two-character width rather than recommending three letters.

The check whose message says 'Null rawTokenId not allowed' actually checks grantType again. Consequently the stated rawTokenId constraint is not enforced, and a null ID is later encoded as the literal 'null'. Check rawTokenId so the diagnostic and constructor contract match the behavior.

This matcher does not verify the expected grant: encodeTokenId places the two-character grant at substring(4, 6), but this checks substring(3, 5) and returns false when it equals the expected value. Consequently, for example, onrtro:<uuid> passes an authorization-code expectation for ac, so the changed event assertions still pass if grant propagation is broken. Check the prefix length and reject when substring(4, 6) does not equal the expected shortcut.

DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId produces session(2) + token(2) + grant(2), so the grant occupies substring(4, 6). This matcher instead examines substring(3, 5) and returns false on equality. Consequently the updated event assertions accept tokens from the wrong grant (for example onrtrt:UUID when expecting ac), defeating the grant-specific checks introduced in this PR. Require equality at the encoder's actual grant offset.

The new factory contract describes a three-letter shortcut, but DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId requires a six-character prefix and reads exactly two characters for the grant. An extension following this interface documentation can issue IDs with a seven-character prefix through encodeTokenId, only for those IDs to be rejected by the decoder. Specify exactly two characters here and validate the width when registering factory shortcuts, or make the encoding format support the documented length.

The constructor checks grantType twice, so a null rawTokenId is accepted despite the explicit non-null constraint. encodeTokenId subsequently concatenates it into the literal string "null", producing a token ID whose decoded raw ID differs from the supplied value. Validate rawTokenId itself to reject this invalid context at construction.

The factory accepts shortcuts of any length, while getTokenContextFromTokenId requires exactly six prefix characters and extracts exactly two for the grant. A custom grant using a three-character shortcut (explicitly suggested by the new factory interface documentation) therefore issues IDs successfully but every such ID throws IllegalArgumentException when decoded. Validate the two-character format during both initial and lazy registration, and align the interface contract with that requirement.

Unlike startup registration, this lazy deployment path does not enforce shortcut uniqueness. If a newly deployed grant reuses an existing shortcut, put replaces its owner while the original grant still maps to that shortcut. Existing tokens then decode as the new grant. Concurrent registrations of two grants sharing a shortcut produce the same corruption. Use atomic ownership checks (including in the decoder's lazy refresh path) and reject collisions rather than replacing an established mapping.

The encoder writes the grant shortcut at indices 4–5 of the six-character prefix, but this matcher reads indices 3–4 and returns false when they equal the expected shortcut. Consequently a valid UUID with an incorrect grant prefix normally passes, so the updated event assertions no longer verify which grant issued the token. Validate the prefix length and reject a mismatch in substring(4, 6).

This repeats the preceding grantType validation instead of checking rawTokenId. A context constructed with a null raw ID is therefore accepted and encodeTokenId serializes it as the literal string "null", rather than rejecting an invalid token identifier as the constructor intends.

issues.descricao: The AccessTokenContext constructor checks grantType twice instead of rawTokenId, so a null rawTokenId passes validation and is encoded as ':null'.
issues.textoGolden: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: the constructor validates `grantType` a second time instead of `rawTokenId` (`Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`). WHY: a null `rawTokenId` is silently accepted, so `encodeTokenId` produces a token id ending in `:null` and any later consumer of the raw id gets an invalid value instead of an early failure. HOW: change the argument to `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`.

Line 73 calls Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed") — it validates grantType a second time (line 72 already does) with a message naming a different field. rawTokenId is never validated, so a null rawTokenId is accepted at construction and the advertised check/message is wrong. It should be Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed").

The null-check message names the wrong parameter: `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` validates `grantType` but reports `rawTokenId`, and it duplicates the check on line 72 while `rawTokenId` is never validated at all. The message that reaches the reader contradicts the code it guards; it should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`.

issues.descricao: isAccessTokenId reads the grant shortcut at the wrong offset (3,5 instead of 4,6) and inverts the comparison, so the event assertions never verify the token's grant type.
issues.textoGolden: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `isAccessTokenId` reads the grant shortcut from the wrong offset and inverts the comparison — `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. WHY: for the encoded id `ssttgg:raw` the grant shortcut occupies 0-based indices 4-5, so `substring(3,5)` inspects the token-type/grant boundary and can never equal the expected shortcut; combined with the inverted `return false`, the equality branch is unreachable and the matcher validates only the UUID part. As a result the new assertions in `expectCodeToToken`/`expectRefresh`/`expectDeviceCodeToToken`/`expectAuthReqIdToToken` do not actually assert the grant type and would pass even if the grant shortcut were wrong. HOW: use `items[0].substring(4, 6)` and negate the condition (`if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`).

The matcher logic is inverted: line 483 returns false when the extracted grant shortcut EQUALS expectedGrantShortcut, so a token that actually carries the expected grant fails the matcher, while a token with any other grant shortcut falls through and passes. The condition should be negated: `if (!items[0].substring(3,5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. Also note the encode site writes the grant shortcut at chars 4-6 (substring(4,6)); substring(3,5) reads one character early into the token-type field, so the offset is off by one relative to TokenManager.encodeTokenId.

The comment 'Grant type shortcut starts at character 4th char' disagrees with the encoding that this PR defines (sessionType chars 1-2, tokenType 3-4, grantType 5-6, e.g. 'trltcc'), and the code reads substring(3,5) — the 4th-5th chars, i.e. the token-type second char plus the grant first char, never the grant shortcut. The comment (and the index) should point at the 5th char / substring(4,6).

issues.descricao: getShortcut() Javadoc says shortcuts are usually 3 letters, but the encoding requires exactly 2-character shortcuts.
issues.textoGolden: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.

comentarios.texto: The Javadoc says getShortcut() returns 'usually like 3-letters shortcut', but every implementation introduced in this PR returns a 2-character shortcut ('ac','cc','pg','pc','rt','ro','te','ci','dg') and the encoder relies on exactly 2 chars (encoded context length 6 = 2+2+2). The doc states a length the code does not produce; it should say 2-character shortcut.

Grant shortcuts are registered without enforcing the two-character length required by the decoder. A custom grant returning a three-character shortcut, which the new OAuth2GrantTypeFactory documentation explicitly suggests, produces a seven-character prefix that getTokenContextFromTokenId rejects, breaking encode/decode round trips for that grant. Validate shortcut length during registration and dynamic refresh, and document the required two-character format.

The new contract describes getShortcut() as usually returning a three-letter shortcut, but DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider requires exactly two characters for the grant field (six total prefix characters, decoded with substring(4, 6)). An extension author following this documentation can produce token IDs that the default decoder rejects. Document the required two-character length rather than advertising three letters.

issues.descricao: testIncorrectGrantType catches any RuntimeException, so it passes on a NullPointerException from the unset sessionFactory rather than verifying the unknown-grant IllegalArgumentException.
issues.textoGolden: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

comentarios.texto: Catching RuntimeException allows this negative test to pass for an unrelated fixture failure. The fixture constructs the factory without postInit, leaving sessionFactory null; resolving the unregistered `ac` shortcut calls sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream and throws NullPointerException before the decoder's intended unknown-grant IllegalArgumentException. Catch/assert IllegalArgumentException specifically and provide a factory fixture whose lookup returns no matching grant, so removing the decoder's validation would fail the test.

issues.descricao: Client-credentials (and UMA permission) token issuance never sets the GRANT_TYPE attribute, so their access token ids are encoded with the unknown grant 'na' instead of their shortcut.

comentarios.texto: The new grant metadata falls back to 'na' for client-credentials and UMA tokens because their issuance paths never set Constants.GRANT_TYPE on their fresh ClientSessionContext. ClientCredentialsGrantType calls responseBuilder.generateAccessToken directly, and PermissionGrantType delegates to AuthorizationTokenService, so neither executes the new assignment in createTokenResponse; tokens from these known grants therefore carry unknown grant context. Set the grant attribute in both issuance paths before generating the access token.

issues.descricao: Lazy registration of newly deployed grants does not check shortcut uniqueness, so a grant reusing an existing shortcut silently overwrites the reverse mapping and older tokens decode to the wrong grant.

comentarios.texto: Enforce shortcut uniqueness during lazy registration rather than overwriting grantsByShortcuts. If a newly deployed grant B uses existing grant A's shortcut, this path replaces shortcut→A with shortcut→B while retaining both forward entries. Previously issued A tokens then decode as B. Concurrent registrations of two new grants with the same shortcut likewise both succeed, with the last inverse-map write winning. Use collision-aware atomic registration and reject the conflicting grant before publishing its forward mapping.

issues.descricao: Claims setFormParams replaces form params without refreshing the cached grantType, leaving getGrantType() stale.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: grantType is snapshotted once from formParams in Context ctor but setFormParams() replaces formParams without refreshing it. WHY: Any caller mutating form params after construction leaves getGrantType() stale, so OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse stores the wrong GRANT_TYPE and encodes the wrong token-id prefix. HOW: Update grantType inside setFormParams or make getGrantType() derive from current formParams.

issues.descricao: getShortcut() is added to OAuth2GrantTypeFactory without a default implementation, breaking existing custom grant type factories when the encoder factory calls it.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: New interface method getShortcut() has no default implementation. WHY: All existing third-party OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations break at runtime/compile (AbstractMethodError) when upgrading, and DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory blindly casts every OAuth2GrantType factory to OAuth2GrantTypeFactory. HOW: Provide a default e.g. default String getShortcut() { return getId(); } or handle missing shortcut.

getShortcut() added as abstract required method breaks existing custom OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations (old contract had no such method). Make it a default method (e.g. default String getShortcut() { return "na"; } or return getId()) or handle null/missing shortcut in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory so legacy providers keep working.

sugestoes.texto: The test asserts caughtExceptions without waiting for the reader thread to finish its in-flight request. A request started during deletion can fail after the assertion, allowing the concurrency regression to pass undetected and leaving work running into test teardown. Keep a reference to the reader and join it after signalling termination, before asserting the collected exceptions.

The reader termination flag is set only after every deletion succeeds. If remove() throws, the test exits with the non-daemon reader still looping, and subsequent client or realm teardown failures are caught and retried indefinitely. Put the deletion loop in a try/finally that always sets the termination flag and waits for the reader to exit.

The stop flag does not wait for the reader to finish. A reader can enter the groups request, the main thread can finish deletion and assert the empty list, and only then can the request fail and append its exception. This lets the regression test pass despite the exact concurrent failure it is intended to detect and leaves a request running after test completion. Retain the thread, stop it in a finally block, and join it before asserting the collected exceptions.

The assertion runs before the reader thread is guaranteed to finish. A groups() request can still be in flight when deletedAll is set, and can throw and append to caughtExceptions after the empty-list assertion has already passed. This lets the regression test report success despite the exact concurrent-read failure it is intended to detect. Retain the reader Thread and join it after setting the stop flag, before checking caughtExceptions.

The reader may still be inside groups() when deletedAll is set. The assertion can therefore observe an empty caughtExceptions list, pass, and only afterward have the reader catch and record a failed request. Reintroducing the getSubGroupsCount failure can thus leave this regression test green. Retain the reader thread and join it after requesting shutdown, before checking caughtExceptions; also ensure the reader has started making requests before deletion begins.

issues.descricao: The cached GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount returns null when the group was deleted concurrently, violating the GroupModel contract that it never returns null and risking NPEs in callers that unbox it.
issues.textoGolden: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `getSubGroupsCount()` now returns `null` when the delegate model is gone, violating the `GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount()` contract whose javadoc (GroupModel.java:296) states 'Never returns null'. WHY: In-repo callers happen to tolerate a Long null, but any caller that unboxes the result (`long c = group.getSubGroupsCount()`) or does arithmetic on it will NPE, converting the old NPE into a different one. HOW: return a non-null sentinel such as `0L` (and assert the empty/absent case explicitly), or update the interface contract to document a nullable return.

getSubGroupsCount() now returns null when the cached delegate is gone (modelSupplier.get() == null), whereas before this change the method delegate-called getGroupModel().getSubGroupsCount(), which could not yield null (a missing delegate surfaced as an exception instead). The declared type Long is now genuinely nullable in a path that previously always produced a value or threw, so any caller that relies on the old contract — unboxing the result (e.g. `group.getSubGroupsCount() > 0`, `long n = group.getSubGroupsCount()`, or passing it to a primitive-typed parameter) — will now throw a NullPointerException instead of getting a value or the previous exception. Since consumers were not updated for the new nullable contract, either keep the non-null behavior for callers that cannot handle null or audit/update every caller of GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount() to null-check before use.

getSubGroupsCount() now returns null when modelSupplier.get() is null, but the count is consumed as a number by brief-representation building; the sibling cache entity changed in this PR (CachedGroup) handles the same 'model unavailable' case by returning a non-null default (getRoleMappings returns Collections.emptySet(), and the subGroups/attributes loaders are built with non-null empty defaults). Returning null here breaks that convention and can surface as an unboxing/NPE on the consumer side of the read path. Return a non-null value (e.g., 0) or only null if the GroupModel contract explicitly declares it nullable.

issues.descricao: The concurrency regression test never waits for the reader thread before asserting no exceptions, so it can pass even when the concurrent-deletion NPE still occurs.
issues.textoGolden: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.

comentarios.texto: The reader thread is started but never synchronized with: the test does not wait for it to complete a read before deleting, and does not join it before asserting caughtExceptions is empty. The deletes can finish before the reader reads at all, or a failing read can land after the assertion, so the test passes even with the bug present. Use a CountDownLatch counted down after the reader's first successful read, start deleting only after it fires, and join the thread (after setting deletedAll) before asserting.

WHAT: The reader thread started at line 139-149 is never joined before `assertThat(caughtExceptions, Matchers.empty())` runs. WHY: The reader can be mid-request when `deletedAll.set(true)` executes; if that request throws (e.g., reading a group deleted concurrently), the exception is appended to `caughtExceptions` AFTER the assertion has already evaluated, so the test can pass even when the NPE regression it targets is present (and is flaky). HOW: after `deletedAll.set(true)`, `thread.join(<timeout>)` (storing the Thread reference) before the assertion.

The reader Thread is started but never joined, so the assertion at line 157 can execute before the reader has completed a single groups() read (or while a read that would throw the NPE is still in flight). If the GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount null-model NullPointerException were reintroduced, this test could still pass because caughtExceptions is asserted empty before the racing reader thread has recorded anything. Capture the Thread, then join it (e.g. Thread reader = new Thread(...); reader.start(); ... deletions ...; deletedAll.set(true); reader.join();) before asserting so the test actually waits on the condition it verifies.

issues.descricao: The reader thread's stop flag is set only after all deletions succeed, so a failing delete leaves a non-daemon thread polling indefinitely.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The reader loop `while (!deletedAll.get())` has no termination guarantee and `deletedAll.set(true)` at line 155 only runs after the delete loop at 152-154 completes. WHY: If any `group(groupUuid).remove()` throws, `deletedAll` is never set, so the non-daemon thread loops forever and the test JVM hangs. HOW: set the thread as daemon and/or wrap deletion in try/finally so `deletedAll.set(true)` always executes.
The test has a mid-loop abort hazard.

The reader's stop flag is set only after every deletion succeeds, with no finally block. If any remove() throws, the test exits with a live non-daemon thread that keeps issuing requests and collecting exceptions indefinitely, interfering with teardown and potentially preventing JVM termination. Put stop signaling and reader termination in a finally block around deletion.

sugestoes.texto:
WHAT: The suffix scan can overlap the prefix already removed from the diagnostic. WHY: For value `aaa
aaa`, sanitization produces `aaaaaa`, both scans consume six characters, and sanitized.substring(6, 0) throws instead of returning a validation error, aborting the Maven verifier. HOW: Limit the suffix scan to the characters remaining after the common prefix in both strings.

WHAT: The message replaces i18next interpolation with Java MessageFormat placeholders and a choice expression. WHY: ThemeResource returns these values unchanged and account-ui uses plain i18next, while setUserProfileServerError supplies numeric interpolation keys, so multivalued validation errors now display literal `{0}`, `{1}`, `{2}` and the choice expression rather than the attribute and limits. HOW: Retain the double-brace placeholders and use wording supported by i18next on this client path; apply the same correction to the admin-ui resource changed in this PR.

WHAT: Normalization removes complete choice expressions, including any HTML in their output branches, before HTML verification. WHY: A translated error-invalid-multivalued-size containing `{2,choice,0#|1#value}` is reduced to `...` and passes this check even though its selectable output contains forbidden markup. HOW: Preserve and validate branch contents instead of replacing the whole expression; exempt only the choice-format separator syntax from HTML interpretation.

WHAT: The Lithuanian OTP setup instruction is replaced with an Italian sentence. WHY: login-config-totp.ftl renders loginTotpStep1 directly, so users selecting Lithuanian now receive their installation instruction in Italian; the account messages_lt.properties change repeats the same error. HOW: Replace the sentence in both Lithuanian bundles with a Lithuanian translation of the new installation instruction.

The suffix scan does not account for the prefix already consumed. For example, an English plain-text key `aa` translated as `a
a` sanitizes to `aa`: the prefix scan consumes one character and the suffix scan consumes both sanitized characters. The diagnostic then calls `sanitized.substring(1, 0)`, throwing an uncaught StringIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of returning the Illegal HTML validation error. Bound the suffix scan by each string's remaining length after `start`, and add a regression test for removed markup between repeated characters.

The suffix scan does not exclude characters already consumed by the prefix scan. For example, a value `><div>` sanitizes to `>` (after unescaping). Both scans consume that single character, so the diagnostic calls `sanitized.substring(1, 0)` and throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of recording illegal HTML. Bound the suffix scan by each string's length minus `start`.

The suffix scan does not exclude characters already consumed by the prefix scan. For example, value `xx` with HTML disallowed sanitizes to `xx`: start becomes 1 and end becomes 2, so sanitized.substring(1, 0) throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. Thus an illegal translation can abort verification instead of producing the intended error. Bound the suffix scan by the remaining lengths after start.

The replacement is Italian, although this bundle is Lithuanian. Users selecting Lithuanian now receive an Italian instruction during OTP setup. The same replacement occurs for totpStep1 in the Lithuanian account bundle; both should retain Lithuanian text while removing the links.
