Workers are created with multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process, whose SpawnProcess class is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process (the default-context Process class). Consequently this check is false for production workers. When a worker exceeds max-unhealthy-seconds, replacement starts without killing the old worker; if the old worker resumes, both flush the same assigned shards and the old worker is no longer tracked. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or the explicit spawn-context class before killing.

When the deadline expires while waiting for one worker, the next iteration breaks before reaching termination for that worker or any subsequent workers. With multiple workers, join(timeout) can therefore return with untracked active flushers, including across consumer rebalances where new flushers can take over the same shards. Stop waiting once the deadline expires, but still run termination cleanup for every worker. The termination guard also needs to recognize the spawn-context workers.

issues.descricao: The wait_produce timer is tagged with 'shards' while sibling flusher metrics use 'shard' for the same value, so per-shard dashboards miss it.
issues.textoGolden: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.

comentarios.texto: The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer is tagged with the key `"shards"`, while the other two metrics emitted in this same loop (`spans.buffer.flusher.produce` at line 185 and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` at line 195) use the key `"shard"`. All three carry the same `shard_tag` value, so this is a pure key-name disagreement: any dashboard or alert that groups/filters by the `shard` tag will silently receive no data from `wait_produce`. Rename the tag key to `"shard"` so all flusher metrics share one tag.

The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer is tagged with key `shards` while every sibling metric introduced/updated in the same method (`spans.buffer.flusher.produce`, `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes`) uses the singular key `shard`. Anything consuming this metric family by the `shard` tag (dashboards, alerts, tag-based aggregation) will silently receive no data for `wait_produce`, and per-shard breakdowns of produce latency will be incomplete. Change the tag to `tags={"shard": shard_tag}` so the tag contract matches the other flusher metrics.

The wait_produce timer tags with "shards", while the sibling metrics in the same loop use "shard" for the same value (shard_tag). Use one tag key, "shard", so queries and dashboards that group by it cover all of these metrics.

issues.descricao: The time.sleep(0.1) added to test_basic to let flusher threads process is a no-op because the test monkeypatches time.sleep.
issues.textoGolden: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The added synchronization point `time.sleep(0.1)` added after the second `step.poll()` is neutralized by the test's own `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at line 15 (same `time` module), so it does not actually wait. WHY: The comment says it 'Give[s] flusher threads time to process after drift change', but the call is a no-op, so the test still races the background flusher thread before `step.join()` and is liable to be flaky / to not exercise the intended post-drift flush path. HOW: Use a non-monkeypatched wait (e.g. capture the real sleep before patching, or use the flusher's thread/process join, or poll until `messages` is non-empty with a real timeout).

The added `time.sleep(0.1)` does not wait: line 15 of the same test does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which replaces `sleep` on the global `time` module, so this call (and the flusher's own `time.sleep`) is a no-op. The comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change' is therefore false — the call returns instantly and provides no synchronisation, so the test does not actually wait for the flusher to process after the drift change. Either synchronise on a real condition (e.g. wait until the expected message is produced) or, if the original `time.sleep` is needed here, patch a module-scoped reference instead of the global `time.sleep`.

The added `time.sleep(0.1)` is a no-op because the test patches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None`, so nothing waits for the flusher threads before `step.join()` and the `messages` assertion. Replace it with a condition-based wait, such as polling until `messages` is non-empty with a deadline. Use the real sleep saved before patching if a delay is needed.

issues.descricao: The restart path only kills a hung flusher if it is a multiprocessing.Process, but spawn-context workers are SpawnProcess, so hung processes are never killed and a duplicate flusher is started for the same shards.
issues.textoGolden: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

comentarios.texto: The new isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard does not match the SpawnProcess instances created by self.mp_context.Process. When a worker hangs, the guard skips kill() and the replacement starts while the original worker remains alive, allowing overlapping flushing of the same shards if the original resumes and leaking hung workers. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or self.mp_context.Process, and kill and join the old worker before replacing it.

The workers are created with get_context("spawn").Process, which produces SpawnProcess instances; these are not instances of multiprocessing.Process (the default-context Process class). Consequently this guard skips kill() for actual production workers. When a worker hangs, the replacement starts while the original remains alive and can resume flushing the same shards. Use multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or the spawn-context Process class for the check, and fix the identical check in join() so shutdown also terminates surviving workers.

Workers created by multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process are SpawnProcess instances, not instances of the separate multiprocessing.Process class. Consequently this guard skips kill() for production workers. When a live worker exceeds max-unhealthy-seconds, the code starts a replacement and overwrites its handle while the original is still running. If the original resumes, both workers flush the same shards, and repeated hangs can exceed the configured process limit. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess (or explicitly distinguish threads) and stop the old worker before replacing it.

issues.descricao: join() breaks out of the per-process loop when the shared deadline expires, skipping termination of the remaining flusher processes and leaving them running after shutdown.
issues.textoGolden: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

comentarios.texto: join() breaks out of the worker loop when the shared deadline expires, skipping cleanup for every remaining worker. If next_step.join consumes the timeout or an earlier worker exhausts it, remaining flushers can continue running after shutdown or partition reassignment. Use the deadline only to limit waiting and still terminate and reap every remaining process.

Do not break out of worker cleanup when the join deadline expires. If the first worker consumes the timeout, the next iteration breaks before terminating that worker or any subsequent workers. They may still be blocked in Redis or producer calls despite the shared stopped flag, leaving old workers running after strategy shutdown/reassignment. Apply the deadline only to waiting, and perform termination cleanup for every worker regardless of remaining time (using a type check that recognizes spawn-context workers).
join() waits for processes sequentially against a single shared deadline and breaks without terminating remaining processes once it expires, leaking them.

issues.descricao: The SpanFlusher docstring says it creates one process per shard, but shards are distributed across at most max_processes processes.

comentarios.texto: The docstring says the flusher "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing," but the code at lines 60-66 shares shards across a capped number of processes (num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards)); each shard assigned via i % self.num_processes). With the new --flusher-processes default of 1, a single process handles every shard, so the documented contract is the opposite of the behaviour this PR introduces (confirmed by test_flusher_processes_limit, which asserts 4 shards served by 2 processes). Update the docstring to say shards are distributed across up to max_processes flusher processes.

The new docstring says this creates one process per shard, but workers are capped by max_processes and shards are distributed among them. In particular, the CLI default of 1 means all assigned shards share one process. Describe capped workers with potentially multiple shards per worker so callers do not rely on per-shard process isolation.

The docstring says the flusher 'Creates one process per shard', but the number of processes is capped by max_processes (--flusher-processes), and shards are shared across processes via i % num_processes. Reword it to say that shards are distributed across at most max_processes processes.

issues.descricao: max_processes uses a truthiness fallback, so --flusher-processes 0 silently becomes one process per shard instead of being rejected.

comentarios.texto: `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats a falsy value as 'not provided'. The new `--flusher-processes` click option is `type=int`, so a user can pass `0`; that legitimate-but-falsy value is discarded and the flusher silently spawns one process per shard instead of honoring the requested limit. Use an explicit None check, e.g. `self.max_processes = max_processes if max_processes is not None else len(buffer.assigned_shards)` (and validate/reject 0 upstream).

An explicit max_processes=0 is treated as an omitted limit by `or`, so passing `--flusher-processes 0` starts one process per assigned shard instead of respecting or rejecting the supplied zero limit. The CLI accepts zero as an integer and the factory forwards it unchanged. Default only when max_processes is None, and explicitly validate that supplied process limits are positive so zero cannot silently enable potentially many workers.

`max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` uses a truthiness test, so an explicit 0 is treated as 'unset' and silently expands to one process per shard. Use `max_processes if max_processes is not None else len(buffer.assigned_shards)` and reject values below 1.

issues.descricao: A negative --flusher-processes value is not validated and makes SpanFlusher construction fail with KeyError.

comentarios.texto: `flusher_processes` is not validated to be >= 1. `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` lets a negative value through (it is truthy), so `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(...))` becomes negative and `range(self.num_processes)` is empty, leaving `process_to_shards_map` as `{}`. The following loop computes `process_index = i % self.num_processes`, which for any negative divisor is 0, so `self.process_to_shards_map[0].append(shard)` raises KeyError and the consumer fails to construct. Since `flusher_processes` is exposed as an int CLI option (`--flusher-processes`), a negative value is reachable from configuration. Guard with `max(1, self.num_processes)` / validate the input.
negative max_processes flows through `or` guard into min() -> empty map -> KeyError on i % num_processes; empty assigned_shards yields zero processes.

issues.descricao: submit() queries cluster-wide Redis memory once per flusher buffer, repeating identical INFO calls per process on every submit.

comentarios.texto: The new loop calls get_memory_info() once per flusher buffer even though SpansBuffer.get_memory_info delegates to iter_cluster_memory_usage(self.client), which fetches INFO for the entire Redis cluster regardless of assigned_shards. With P flusher processes and memory backpressure enabled, each submitted batch now performs P identical cluster-wide memory queries on the consumer thread instead of one, increasing Redis traffic and blocking ingestion. Fetch cluster memory information once from a single buffer.
submit() loop calls buffer.get_memory_info() per flusher but each call is cluster-wide from same client, repeating identical INFO N× per submit.

issues.descricao: _create_process_for_shard is added but never called.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is newly added but has no caller anywhere (grep for `_create_process_for_shard(` finds only its definition); the restart path actually used is `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`. WHY: This is dead code that indicates the intended per-shard restart wiring was left incomplete — any future caller relying on restarting only the process owning a given shard will silently do nothing, and it is confusing which restart path is authoritative. HOW: Remove `_create_process_for_shard`, or wire it into `_ensure_processes_alive` if per-shard restart was intended.

issues.descricao: test_flusher_processes_limit counts assigned shards instead of checking that each shard is assigned exactly once.

comentarios.texto: The assertion counts shard entries rather than verifying shard assignment. A broken distribution such as {0: [0, 1], 1: [0, 1]} still passes all assertions in this test while shards 2 and 3 are never flushed. Assert that the flattened mapping contains exactly the expected assigned shards, with no duplicates (and verify each worker's shard buffer uses that mapping), rather than only asserting a total of four.

issues.descricao: Splitting the buffer per process makes spans.buffer.max-flush-segments a per-process cap, so with P flusher processes up to P times the configured segments are loaded and flushed per cycle.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Splitting the single buffer into per-process SpansBuffer(shards) instances breaks the global 'spans.buffer.max-flush-segments' cap, because SpansBuffer.flush_segments computes max_segments_per_shard = ceil(max_flush_segments / len(self.assigned_shards)) using only the subset of shards given to that sub-buffer. WHY: The option is documented as 'Maximum number of segments to fetch and flush per cycle' (default 500), but with P flusher processes each sub-buffer gets max_flush_segments×(total_shards/P)/total_shards per shard and flushes up to max_flush_segments, so the aggregate cap becomes P×500 per cycle — multiplying memory loaded from Redis by the process count and also making any_shard_at_limit backpressure P× harder to trigger, exactly when the flusher is being scaled up. HOW: Either keep a single shared cap (e.g. compute num per shard from the total shard count, or pass the intended per-shard budget explicitly / divide by the total number of processes) so the per-cycle total is not multiplied by the number of flusher processes.

issues.descricao: Claims the CLI default of 1 makes the one-process-per-shard auto mode unreachable.

comentarios.texto: The click option declares `default=1` for `flusher_processes`, but the consumer this feeds (SpanFlusher, via ProcessSpansStrategyFactory) is designed around `None` meaning "auto = one process per shard" (`self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`). Because the producer always passes 1, the `or` fallback never fires and the flusher is permanently capped at a single process for all shards, silently disabling the one-process-per-shard parallelism this PR introduces. The default should be `None` (or the flusher sentinel respected) so auto-scaling is actually reachable; as written the advertised behavior is dead in production.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: The queued default is evaluated once when the module is imported rather than when an AssignmentSource is created. WHY: Every inbound assignment in a long-lived worker receives the same stale timestamp, and from_dict also uses that timestamp when queued is omitted, so the carrier does not record when the assignment was queued. HOW: Use a dataclass default factory to evaluate timezone.now for each instance.

The empty-array test passes `{}`, not `[]`. It therefore exercises missing constructor arguments rather than rejection of a non-mapping input. A regression that accepts an empty list would leave this test passing. Supply an empty list to test the named case (and retain a separately named empty-dictionary case if desired).

The dataclass default calls timezone.now() once when the module is imported, not for each new assignment source. Consequently sources created hours later (including all from_integration calls) serialize the same stale queued timestamp rather than the time of the assignment. Use a default_factory so this timestamp reflects each source's creation time, and test creation at two distinct mocked times.

issues.descricao: AssignmentSource.queued defaults to timezone.now() evaluated at class definition, so all instances share the import-time timestamp instead of the time they were queued.
issues.textoGolden: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` evaluates once at class-definition time so every AssignmentSource without explicit queued shares the same timestamp. WHY: queued time is wrong/stale for all later instances and defeats its purpose as a queue-time marker. HOW: use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` (with `field` import).

Field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at import so all AssignmentSources share the same timestamp. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each instance measures its actual creation/queue time.

The dataclass field default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated a single time when the module is imported, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit `queued` value (which is exactly what `from_integration` does, and what `from_dict` falls back to when the key is absent) shares the same frozen import-time timestamp instead of the moment the assignment was actually queued. This makes the `queued` timestamp semantically wrong/meaningless (it reflects process start, not assignment time) and would silently misreport the queue time anywhere this value is later inspected. Fix by defaulting in a factory/`__post_init__` or making the caller pass the timestamp, e.g. set `queued` inside `from_integration` (`queued=timezone.now()`), or use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

issues.descricao: The test method name test_from_dict_inalid_data has a typo; it should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
issues.textoGolden: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.

comentarios.texto: Typo in test name test_from_dict_inalid_data hides it from name-filtered runs (e.g. -k invalid_data): fix spelling to test_from_dict_invalid_data so the invalid-payload guard is actually selected and verified.

issues.descricao: test_from_dict_empty_array actually passes an empty dict, so the name does not match what the test exercises.
issues.textoGolden: Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

comentarios.texto: The test is named test_from_dict_empty_array but it passes an empty dict ({}), not an empty array; a caller reading the name will believe the empty-list/array input path is covered when it is not. Rename it to test_from_dict_empty_dict (or pass [] to actually cover the empty-array case) so the identifier agrees with the input it exercises.

test_from_dict_empty_array names an empty array but constructs an empty dict (`data: dict[str, Any] = {}`), so it only re-exercises the empty/None path and never covers empty-array input; a regression specific to that input would pass unnoticed. Pass a real empty array or rename the test to match its body.

test_from_dict_empty_array passes {} rather than an empty array. It therefore only tests missing required dictionary keys and would still pass if rejection of an array input were broken. Pass [] to exercise the named case (or rename this test to empty_dict if that is the intended contract).

issues.descricao: Claims to_dict() returns a raw datetime for queued that fails JSON serialization when passed as Celery task kwargs.
issues.textoGolden: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.

comentarios.texto: `to_dict` uses `asdict`, which leaves `queued` as a raw `datetime` object in the dict. That dict is passed straight into a celery task kwarg in `sync_group_assignee_outbound` (`assignment_source_dict=assignment_source.to_dict()`), i.e. it is the payload crossing the serialization boundary. Send a serializable form instead (e.g. `queued.isoformat()` / `queued.timestamp()`), and make `from_dict` parse it back to a `datetime`, so the value survives the queue round trip instead of raising at encode time or arriving as a string where the annotation promises a datetime.

`to_dict` emits `queued` as a raw `datetime` (dataclass field default in from_integration is a live timezone.now() value), but this dict is placed into `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs=...)` in src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py:137-144 and serialized by the Celery task serializer on the way to the consumer in src/sentry/integrations/tasks/sync_assignee_outbound.py, which reconstructs it via `AssignmentSource.from_dict`. A datetime is not JSON-native, so the value either fails to serialize at enqueue (breaking outbound propagation to other integrations) or comes back as a plain string, so `from_dict` builds an AssignmentSource whose `queued` silently violates the declared `datetime` type. Serialize `queued` explicitly (e.g. `datetime.isoformat()`) in `to_dict` and parse it back in `from_dict` so the producer and consumer agree on the representation.

WHAT: `to_dict()` via `asdict()` returns a raw `datetime` for `queued`, which is then passed as Celery task kwargs in `sync_group_assignee_outbound` (`assignment_source.to_dict()`). WHY: datetime is not JSON-serializable for the task serializer and round-trips back as a string that `from_dict` never parses, leaving `queued` as str type or crashing serialization. HOW: serialize `queued` to ISO string in `to_dict` and parse it back in `from_dict`.

issues.descricao: The assignment_source parameter was added to the abstract sync_status_outbound instead of sync_assignee_outbound, which is the method that actually receives it.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `assignment_source` param was added to `sync_status_outbound` instead of `sync_assignee_outbound`, while the task calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=...)` whose abstract declares only `**kwargs`. WHY: concrete `sync_assignee_outbound` overrides without `**kwargs` will raise TypeError on the new kwarg, and the status method gains a dead param that is never checked. HOW: declare `assignment_source` explicitly on `sync_assignee_outbound` abstract (and update overrides) and remove it from `sync_status_outbound` unless status sync needs the same guard.

issues.descricao: Claims concrete integrations overriding should_sync(self, attribute) will raise TypeError at the new two-argument call in sync_assignee_outbound.

comentarios.texto: The outbound task now calls `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` with a second argument. This PR updated the two base implementations (`IssueBasicIntegration.should_sync` and `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync` in mixins/issues.py) to accept it, but any concrete integration that overrides `should_sync` with the pre-PR signature `(self, attribute)` was not updated. Such an override still works for the existing 1-arg caller `where_should_sync` (sync.py:48), but at this new 2-arg call site it raises `TypeError: should_sync() takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given`, crashing the assignee-outbound task for that provider. Verify all `should_sync` overrides accept the new parameter (or pass it as a keyword so the mismatch is at least explicit), otherwise this call breaks them at runtime.

issues.descricao: Claims a malformed assignment_source_dict makes from_dict return None, so should_sync fails open and re-enables the sync cycle.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `AssignmentSource.from_dict()` returns None on invalid/extra/missing keys and the task treats None as no-source, so `should_sync('outbound_assignee', None)` returns True. WHY: a corrupt or tampered `assignment_source_dict` fails open and re-enables the outbound sync the PR intends to suppress, resuming the cycle. HOW: distinguish parse-failure from absent source (log + skip sync, or fail closed).

issues.descricao: test_to_dict asserts queued is not None, which is always true because queued has a default, so the assertion verifies nothing.

comentarios.texto: test_to_dict asserts `result.get("queued") is not None`, but `queued` always has a default value, so the assertion cannot fail. Pass an explicit `queued` datetime and assert that to_dict returns exactly that value, or compare the whole dict.

sugestoes.texto: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature, which Pipeline.__init__ derives solely from pipeline view class names rather than a session-specific random value. An attacker can obtain an OAuth code for their own GitHub account and inject it with the known shared state into another user's active installation pipeline, causing that pipeline to accept the attacker's GitHub identity. Generate a cryptographically random nonce, persist it in pipeline state before redirecting, and compare the callback against that nonce.

The new installer check indexes integration.metadata['sender'] without handling integrations that lack sender metadata. build_integration only adds sender when supplied in state, while the browser pipeline can create integrations without it; reconnecting such an integration after its organization association is removed now raises KeyError instead of returning the installation error. Read sender defensively and reject the request with the existing error response when installer metadata is unavailable.

When the supplied installation ID has no Integration row (for example, before the installation webhook has been processed), Integration.DoesNotExist advances the pipeline immediately. Consequently the authenticated GitHub login is never checked against the installer, although build_integration subsequently fetches the installation using this supplied ID. OAuth authentication alone does not establish ownership of that installation. Apply an ownership check on this path too, or reject/retry until the webhook-created installation and its sender are available; otherwise the authenticity check depends on webhook timing.

The call to safe_urlopen occurs before the try block. If GitHub is unavailable, times out, or returns a non-success HTTP response, the exchange raises rather than returning the installation error page. Every GitHub installation now passes through this request, so these failures terminate the setup callback with an unhandled exception. Include the token request in the guarded exchange and handle the expected HTTP/transport exceptions with the existing error response.

The new validation unconditionally reads integration.metadata['sender']['login'], but build_integration still only writes sender when state.get('sender') is present (and installation.py explicitly recognizes integrations lacking it). An active integration without an OrganizationIntegration and without sender metadata previously proceeded through this path; it now raises KeyError and returns a server error instead of completing or showing the invalid-installation response. Handle absent sender metadata explicitly, failing closed with the existing error response or obtaining authoritative installer information before comparing.

The helper translates a variable, but its default short message and the short-message literals supplied by callers are not marked for translation. Django's message extraction cannot discover strings through _(error_short), so the new "Invalid installation request." message will not enter translation catalogs, and the two previously marked messages lose their extraction sites. Mark the default and each call-site literal with _(), and pass the resulting lazy message through unchanged in the payload.

test_installation_not_found now sends state `ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05` rather than the pipeline state used by the other flows and asserts `Invalid installation request.` OAuthLoginView returns that error on a state mismatch before GitHubInstallation or the stubbed installation 404 is reached. Consequently this test still passes if missing installations are mishandled or the installation lookup is removed. Complete OAuth with the actual pipeline state and assert the installation-specific failure so the configured 404 is exercised.

`pipeline.signature` is not an authorization nonce: pipeline/base.py derives it from the pipeline view class names using MD5. Consequently all users of this pipeline share a predictable state (the tests likewise use the same literal across users). An attacker can initiate GitHub authorization for their own account and deliver its callback code with this known state to a victim with an active installation pipeline, allowing login CSRF/account substitution. Generate a cryptographically random state for each authorization attempt, store it in the victim's pipeline/session, and validate and consume it on callback rather than using the pipeline fingerprint.

issues.descricao: error() calls _(error_short) on a variable and callers pass plain literals, so the short error strings are no longer extractable for translation.

comentarios.texto: The helper calls `_(error_short)` on a variable, and callers pass plain string literals. The translation extractor cannot see these strings, so the short error messages sent to the user are no longer translatable; the old code wrapped the literals directly in `_()`. Mark the literals with gettext_lazy at the call sites and the default, and pass them through without wrapping again.

error_short strings bypass translation extraction: _(error_short) uses a variable so makemessages cannot collect them. Wrap literals at definition/call sites, e.g. error_short=_("Invalid installation request.") and pass _("...") literals, then use data error value directly without re-wrapping.

Translate the short-message literals at their definition/call sites instead of calling `_(error_short)` on a variable. Django's message extraction cannot extract the default `"Invalid installation request."` or the plain-string arguments at the two call sites from this dynamic gettext invocation. The existing pending-deletion and already-installed messages previously appeared directly inside `_()`; this refactor removes their extraction sites, and the new default message cannot enter translation catalogs. Use a translated default and translated arguments, then place `error_short` directly into the payload so these user-facing errors remain localizable.

issues.descricao: The org parameter of error()/get_document_origin is actually the active-organization context, not an Organization, so the name is misleading.

comentarios.texto: The parameter is named `org` but the code treats it as the pipeline's active-organization context: it dereferences `org.organization` and every caller (error() and the GitHubInstallation sites) passes `self.active_organization`, not an Organization. The name misstates the argument's type/contract — a caller following the name and passing a real Organization would hit AttributeError on `.organization`. Rename the parameter (e.g. `active_organization`) and correct the corresponding name in `error()` at line 131 so the two signatures match what is actually passed.

issues.descricao: The GitHub OAuth state is pipeline.signature, a static md5 of the pipeline view names, instead of a per-attempt random nonce, so it gives no CSRF protection.
issues.textoGolden: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

comentarios.texto: The OAuth state is pipeline.signature, which Pipeline.__init__ computes solely from pipeline view class names and therefore shares across all users and installation attempts. An attacker can obtain an OAuth code for their own GitHub account and send a callback using this known state to a victim with an active installation pipeline, binding the attacker's GitHub identity to the victim's flow instead of rejecting the forged callback. Generate a random per-attempt nonce, store it in pipeline state, and validate that nonce on the OAuth callback.

Do not use pipeline.signature as OAuth state. It is a deterministic MD5 of the pipeline identifiers, not an unpredictable nonce tied to this user's authorization attempt (the tests reuse it across users). An attacker can know the expected state and submit a callback containing a code authorized under the attacker's GitHub account, defeating the OAuth login-CSRF protection and the intended binding to the installing user. Generate a cryptographically random per-attempt state, store it in the session/pipeline, and validate and consume it on callback.

issues.descricao: The new OAuth step's token exchange and user lookup are not wrapped in error handling, so GitHub/network failures surface as 500s instead of the installation-failed page.

comentarios.texto: The token request is executed outside the try block. If GitHub's token endpoint is unavailable or the request fails with a connection/timeout error, safe_urlopen raises before the guarded response parsing is reached, and this new installation step returns an unhandled server error instead of the installation-failed response. Include the request itself in the error handling and handle the relevant transport exceptions.

WHAT: safe_urlopen token exchange and get_user_info() (which calls resp.raise_for_status()) are called with no exception handling. WHY: Any network error, timeout, or non-2xx from GitHub bubbles up as an unhandled exception and 500s the install instead of rendering the invalid-request page. HOW: Wrap the exchange plus get_user_info in try/except and return error() on failure.

safe_urlopen() and get_user_info() are called outside any try/except, so network errors, non-2xx responses, or API failures raise unhandled exceptions instead of returning error(). Wrap the token exchange + user-info fetch in try/except and return error() on failure, matching the handled missing-access_token path.

issues.descricao: When no Integration exists yet for the installation_id the pipeline advances without comparing the OAuth user to the installer, bypassing the new ownership check.

comentarios.texto: The missing Integration branch advances the pipeline without verifying that github_authenticated_user installed the supplied installation_id. When the installation webhook has not created a record, or the local record was deleted, finish_pipeline calls build_integration using app credentials and attaches the installation without checking the OAuth user's access, allowing a user with another account's installation ID to bypass the new ownership check. Fail closed until trusted installer information is available and apply the ownership check before every successful next_step.

The record-absent path advances the pipeline before checking whether the authenticated GitHub user installed this app. Installation IDs arrive from the request, and a missing Integration record (for example before the installation webhook is processed) does not establish ownership. As a result, this path can attach an installation belonging to a different GitHub user despite the new authenticity check. Verify the authenticated user's authorization for the installation before advancing in this branch too, rather than relying on the webhook-created record existing.

When no Integration row exists for the installation_id, the code calls next_step() without comparing the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user to the installer. An attacker can supply an installation_id they do not own before the installation webhook has created the row, and bypass the new verification. Do not skip the check in this branch. Either fail closed, or verify ownership another way, for example by confirming the user can access the installation through the GitHub API.

issues.descricao: The installer check indexes integration.metadata['sender']['login'] without checking that sender exists, raising KeyError for integrations created without sender metadata.
issues.textoGolden: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation

comentarios.texto: integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] is indexed without checking that "sender" exists, so an ACTIVE integration whose metadata has no sender raises KeyError (500) here. metadata["sender"] is only populated when state.get("sender") is set (integration.py:376-377), and the only writer of that state is the installation webhook (webhook.py:202-208); integrations created through the pipeline itself carry no sender (confirmed by installation.py:44 which explicitly guards `if "sender" not in integration.metadata`, and by the pipeline-created integration in test_integration.py:730-743). Previously this branch only bound state and called pipeline.next_step(), so this crash is newly introduced. Fix: guard the lookup, e.g. `if pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != (integration.metadata.get("sender") or {}).get("login"):` and decide the desired fallback when sender is absent.

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` can raise KeyError. build_integration (line 376-377) only sets metadata["sender"] when state.get("sender") is truthy, so an existing Integration without a sender entry makes this subscripting throw an unhandled KeyError (500) instead of routing to the intended error page. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` (and treat a missing sender as a failed verification) so the mismatch/absence case returns error() rather than crashing.

The new ownership check indexes integration.metadata['sender']['login'] even though GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration omits sender for normal pipeline-created integrations. Reconnecting an existing active integration without an OrganizationIntegration and without webhook-populated sender now raises KeyError and returns a server error rather than an installation failure. Handle missing sender explicitly and return the invalid-installation response when trusted installer metadata is unavailable.

issues.descricao: test_installation_not_found uses a wrong OAuth state, so it fails at the state check and never reaches the installation-not-found path it is meant to test.

comentarios.texto: First response (installation_id) is overwritten by second response (bad state) with no assertion, so the Integration.DoesNotExist / not-ACTIVE branch in GitHubInstallation is never verified. Keep/assert the first flow through a valid OAuth step to reach the installation check instead of only asserting the OAuth state-mismatch error.

This test no longer verifies the "installation not found" path it exists for. The second GET supplies state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05, which is not the github pipeline signature (that is the 9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3 asserted in test_github_setup and reused elsewhere). OAuthLoginView.dispatch (integration.py:412-413) therefore returns error() before GitHubInstallation runs, producing the same generic "Invalid installation request." message and the same failed template via the state-mismatch branch. The Integration.DoesNotExist handling at integration.py:493-498 is never reached, so the test would still pass if that handling were removed or broken. Use the real pipeline state so the request advances into GitHubInstallation, or assert on something that distinguishes the state-mismatch branch from the missing-installation branch.

The replacement assertion no longer verifies that a nonexistent installation is rejected: 'Invalid installation request.' is also returned for a state mismatch, missing access token, or missing authenticated login before GitHubInstallation is reached. This test can therefore pass with installation-not-found handling broken if the callback fails OAuth validation instead. Establish a successful OAuth exchange with the actual pipeline state and verify that the nonexistent installation lookup is reached and rejected, rather than accepting this shared authentication-error message alone.

issues.descricao: Claims the OAuth state is compared to the secret pipeline signature in non-constant time, leaking timing information.

comentarios.texto: The OAuth `state` value is compared to the secret per-flow `pipeline.signature` with a plain `!=` string comparison, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and leaks a prefix-match timing signal about the state nonce. Since this check is the CSRF/authenticity guard for the install flow, use a constant-time comparison (e.g. `hmac.compare_digest(request.GET.get("state", ""), pipeline.signature)` / `sentry.utils.security.constant_time_compare`) instead of `!=`.

The OAuth `state` value is compared to `pipeline.signature` with a plain `!=`, which is not a constant-time comparison of a secret token. Use `django.utils.crypto.constant_time_compare(request.GET.get("state", ""), pipeline.signature)` instead.

issues.descricao: Claims other consumers driving GitHubInstallation without the new OAuth view will always be rejected; no such consumer exists.

comentarios.texto: GitHubInstallation now refuses the installation unless the pipeline already carries `github_authenticated_user`, but that state is produced only by the newly prepended OAuthLoginView (see the `get_pipeline_views` change at line 344). Any caller that drives this provider's second step without the new preceding OAuth view — e.g. a subclass/related provider that reuses `GitHubInstallation` (or keeps a GitHubInstallation-only `get_pipeline_views`) — will have `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")` evaluate to None, never match `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`, and always render the ERR_INTEGRATION_INVALID_INSTALLATION_REQUEST failure page. The install path that previously succeeded is now unconditionally rejected for those consumers. Either update every consumer to include OAuthLoginView in its pipeline, or make the authenticity check fall back when the OAuth step was not part of the pipeline.

issues.descricao: Claims a null reference when the github_authenticated_user state is missing; the code only compares it and returns the error page.
issues.textoGolden: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing

issues.descricao: test_github_user_mismatch asserts only the generic 'Invalid installation request.' message, which any error path would produce.

comentarios.texto: test_github_user_mismatch asserts only the generic 'Invalid installation request.' message, which every error() path in OAuthLoginView and GitHubInstallation returns. A wrong hardcoded state, a token failure or a missing integration would pass it just as well as a real sender/login mismatch. Make the mismatch the only possible failure: derive the state from the actual pipeline signature, and assert that the same flow succeeds when the webhook sender is 'octocat'.

sugestoes.texto: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now inherits four abstract members from StatefulDetectorHandler without implementing them. Accessing detector.detector_handler for a metric_alert_fire detector invokes this class in models/detector.py and raises TypeError, aborting process_detectors instead of preserving the previous no-op behavior. Keep this placeholder on DetectorHandler with an evaluate method returning an empty dict until the stateful methods are implemented.

Changing this empty class to inherit StatefulDetectorHandler makes it abstract: it implements neither get_dedupe_value nor get_group_key_values nor the newly required build_occurrence_and_event_data. When a metric-alert Detector's detector_handler property constructs the registered handler, Python raises TypeError before evaluation can run. Previously this handler was concrete and safely returned no results. Keep the concrete no-op handler until the stateful hooks are implemented, or implement all required hooks before switching the base class.

Changing this subclass to StatefulDetectorHandler makes it abstract: that base requires counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the newly added build_occurrence_and_event_data. Unlike the updated test subclass, this class implements none of them. Instantiating the registered metric-alert detector handler will therefore raise TypeError rather than evaluating the packet. Keep the concrete no-op DetectorHandler implementation (returning an empty dictionary for the new evaluate contract) until the stateful methods are implemented.

Changing this concrete handler to StatefulDetectorHandler leaves get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the newly required build_occurrence_and_event_data abstract. Accessing Detector.detector_handler for the metric-alert group type therefore raises TypeError during handler construction, before process_detectors can evaluate it; previously this handler could be instantiated and returned an empty list. Keep the placeholder concrete with the updated dictionary evaluation contract until its stateful hooks are implemented.

The new occurrence test double ignores `value`, making the assertions insensitive to whether `evaluate_group_key_value` forwards the actual measurement to `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. In `test_state_results_multi_group`, group_2 has value 10 but the expected occurrence is built with 6, and the test still passes. A regression that passes a constant or reuses the first group's value therefore goes undetected. Include the value in the generated evidence data (and use 10 for the second expected occurrence), or assert the hook's arguments explicitly.

The docstring immediately below still says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but this change returns a dictionary keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Callers following that documentation and iterating the return value will get keys rather than evaluation results. Update the docstring to describe the mapping contract.

The preceding TODO says this will become a stateful detector when that abstraction is built, but the class now inherits that very abstraction. Remove or revise the TODO so readers are not told the stateful abstraction is still missing.

issues.descricao: The TODO above MetricAlertDetectorHandler says it will become a stateful detector, but the class already subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler.

comentarios.texto: The comment 'TODO: This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction' is now stale. MetricAlertDetectorHandler already subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler. Remove or reword the TODO.

Remove or revise the adjacent TODO saying this will become a stateful detector 'when we build that abstraction'. The class now inherits StatefulDetectorHandler, so the comment describes already-completed work as a future migration and misleads maintainers about which abstraction this handler uses.

issues.descricao: MetricAlertDetectorHandler subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler without implementing its abstract methods, so instantiating it for metric alert detectors raises TypeError where it previously returned an empty-result handler.
issues.textoGolden: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler with an empty body, so it does not implement the abstract methods counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and build_occurrence_and_event_data declared on StatefulDetectorHandler. WHY: the class is now abstract, and Detector.detector_handler (src/sentry/workflow_engine/models/detector.py:86) instantiates it via group_type.detector_handler(self), so any detector whose type resolves to this grouptype will raise TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler — the previous version implemented evaluate and was instantiable. HOW: implement the required abstract methods (or keep a concrete evaluate override) so the handler can be constructed.

MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler but with `pass`, so it implements none of the abstract methods it inherits (counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the newly added build_occurrence_and_event_data). The class is therefore still abstract and instantiating it (it is registered as `detector_handler` on MetricAlertFire and is constructed by Detector.detector_handler) raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...`. Before this change it subclassed DetectorHandler and implemented the single abstract `evaluate`, so it was instantiable; the PR makes the metric-alert handler path throw. Either implement the required abstract methods or keep the class free of unimplemented abstracts.

MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler (an abc.ABC) with only `pass`. StatefulDetectorHandler declares four abstract methods — counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the newly added build_occurrence_and_event_data (detector.py:142-170) — none of which are implemented here. The class therefore remains abstract and cannot be instantiated; Detector.detector_handler's `group_type.detector_handler(self)` will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler` for the metric_alert_fire group type. Previously this class was a concrete DetectorHandler with an implemented evaluate, so this PR newly makes it uninstantiable. Implement the required abstract methods (or revert to a concrete handler) to satisfy the base-class contract.

issues.descricao: The evaluate() docstring says it returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but it now returns a dict keyed by group key.
issues.textoGolden: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.

comentarios.texto: Update evaluate's adjacent docstring to describe a dictionary keyed by DetectorGroupKey rather than a list of DetectorEvaluationResult. This change returns a dictionary and callers now consume .values(), but the documented return contract still tells readers to expect a list; iterating the documented result as a list would instead yield group keys.
Docstring says 'returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult' but signature/body now return dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]. Update docstring to describe dict keyed by group_key.

The evaluate() docstring still says it returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`. The method now returns a dict mapping group key to `DetectorEvaluationResult`. Update the docstring to describe the dict return shape.

issues.descricao: The mock occurrence builder ignores its value argument, so tests (e.g. group_2 expected with 6 while the packet carries 10) pass regardless of which value is passed to build_occurrence_and_event_data.
issues.textoGolden: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.

comentarios.texto: The new occurrence builder accepts `value` but never incorporates or asserts it, so the occurrence tests cannot detect incorrect forwarding of the measured value to `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. For example, `test_state_results_multi_group` supplies 10 for group_2 but builds its expected occurrence with 6 and still passes. A regression that passes a constant or another group's measurement at the new production hook would therefore go unnoticed. Include the value in the mock occurrence's evidence and use the actual expected measurement, or assert the hook's arguments directly.

`build_mock_occurrence_and_event` accepts `value: int` but never uses it (the occurrence is built only from `group_key`/`new_status`), and this same helper is also the implementation of `MockDetectorStateHandler.build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Because neither the expected occurrence nor the handler output depends on the value, tests like `test_state_results_multi_group` (which incorrectly builds the group_2 occurrence with `value=6` while the packet carries `10`) and `TestEvaluate.test_dedupe` (expected built with 6 vs packet 8) pass regardless of the value actually passed into `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. If evaluation passed a wrong value, these tests would still pass, so they do not verify the value/threshold path they appear to cover. Include `value` in a field of the occurrence (or assert on it in the handler) and fix the wrong expected values so the argument is actually checked.

`build_mock_occurrence_and_event` accepts a `value: int` parameter but never uses it — the returned IssueOccurrence is derived only from `group_key` and `new_status`. Because `value` is dead, callers can pass a mismatched value with no failure: in `test_state_results_multi_group` the packet contains `group_2: 10`, but the expected occurrence for `group_2` is built with `6`. Either use `value` when constructing the occurrence so the test validates the group value, or drop the unused parameter and pass the correct value; otherwise the test silently accepts wrong group values.

issues.descricao: get_failure_reason's docstring examples do not match the strings the function returns.

comentarios.texto: The `get_failure_reason` docstring describes output this function does not produce. The singular branch (line 146) returns a `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP` value such as "A missed check-in was detected", yet the docstring advertises "A failed check-in was detected"; the multi-check-in branch joins `"%(count)d %(status)s"` fragments with `get_text_list(..., last_word=_("and"))` and appends " check-ins detected", yielding "2 missed and 1 error check-ins detected", not the docstring's "2 missed check-ins, 1 timeout check-in and 1 error check-in were detected". Update the examples (or the format string) so the documented contract matches the code.

The get_failure_reason docstring examples don't match the output. It shows 'A failed check-in was detected' and '...were detected', but the code returns the per-status singular strings ('A missed check-in was detected') or '<list> check-ins detected'. Update the examples to the real output and fix the 'humam readible' typo.

issues.descricao: get_monitor_environment_context builds a config copy with the human-readable schedule_type but returns the original monitor.config, so the conversion is lost and the context shows the raw value.
issues.textoGolden: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: get_monitor_environment_context copies monitor.config to `config` and converts schedule_type display, but returns the original monitor_environment.monitor.config instead of `config`. WHY: the display conversion never takes effect so the occurrence context carries the raw schedule_type value, producing wrong output vs the function's evident intent. HOW: return `"config": config` instead of `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config`.

Dead computation: `config` is copied and `config['schedule_type']` transformed to display value, but return uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (original) instead of `config`. Change to `"config": config` so transformation is used.

WHAT: In get_monitor_environment_context the code copies config and replaces config['schedule_type'] with the human-readable get_schedule_type_display(), but the returned context dict uses the original `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of the modified local `config`, so the mutation is dead. WHY: The occurrence's monitor context always reports the raw schedule_type value rather than the display string the code intended to substitute, producing incorrect evidence data in the emitted occurrence. HOW: return the local variable, i.e. use "config": config in the returned dict.

issues.descricao: Claims previous_checkins[0] can raise IndexError when the threshold query returns no rows.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: starting_checkin = previous_checkins[0] indexes without an empty-list guard when the threshold>1 query returns no rows. WHY: raises IndexError and crashes the mark_failed/consumer path when the failed check-in is not visible to the date_added__lte filter (unsaved/synthetic check-in, clock skew, or race). HOW: guard with if not previous_checkins: return False before indexing.

issues.descricao: Asks to confirm no consumer still imports SimpleCheckIn from mark_failed after it moved to monitors/types.py.

comentarios.texto: `SimpleCheckIn` was moved out of `src/sentry/monitors/logic/mark_failed.py` into this module. Any consumer that still does `from sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed import SimpleCheckIn` (the old home of this symbol) will now fail with an ImportError at module load. The new in-tree consumers (`monitors/logic/incidents.py`, `monitors/logic/incident_occurrence.py`) were updated to import from `sentry.monitors.types`, but confirm there is no other importer left referencing the old location (e.g. tests or addon code); if there is, update it to import `SimpleCheckIn` from `sentry.monitors.types`.

issues.descricao: Claims fetching MonitorCheckIn objects by id is an unnecessary query because previous_checkins already has the data.
issues.textoGolden: The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: A matching date override returns true before checking the host's busy intervals. WHY: Both fixed-host and round-robin checks pass busy calendar and booking intervals into this function, but every slot on an override day bypasses those conflicts, exposing already occupied times as available. HOW: Let a valid override bypass only the recurring-working-hours check, then continue to busy.every instead of returning true.

WHAT: The working-hours check rejects a slot when it lies outside any interval for that weekday instead of accepting it when it fits one interval. WHY: For a host with 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00 availability, a 10:00 slot fails against the afternoon interval and a 14:00 slot fails against the morning interval, removing valid slots even for single-host events. HOW: Require containment in at least one matching weekday interval, using slotEndTime for the end boundary, and reject when none matches.

WHAT: Override validation tests whether the slot is wholly before or starts after the interval rather than requiring full containment. WHY: In a round-robin event, another host can generate a 09:30–10:30 or 10:30–11:30 slot while a fixed host's override is only 10:00–11:00; both slots pass this check despite the fixed host being unavailable for part of the meeting. HOW: Accept only slots whose start is at or after the override start and whose end is at or before the override end.

WHAT: Converted override boundaries are reduced to hour/minute values without preserving date rollover. WHY: A UTC organizer's 20:00–23:00 override viewed at UTC+2 becomes startTime 1320 and endTime 60; buildSlots discards it because start >= end, so the valid 22:00–24:00 portion disappears. Intervals shifted wholly across midnight are instead attached to the original invitee day. HOW: Convert full override instants, intersect them with each invitee day, and derive minute boundaries from those clipped intervals rather than wrapping each endpoint independently.

The fixed- and loose-host filtering callers still rely on checkIfIsAvailable to reject slots overlapping `schedule.busy`, but this new early return accepts every slot within a matching date override before reaching `busy.every(...)`. Thus a host with an override and an existing booking or calendar conflict on that date can now be presented as available. Previously this predicate always checked busy periods (apart from the explicit current-seats exception). A matching override should bypass the normal working-hours check, not the busy-calendar check.

When a slot falls on a date override and passes the override boundary checks, this early return skips `busy.every(...)` entirely. For example, an override permitting 09:00–17:00 and an existing booking at 10:00–11:00 now cause the 10:00 slot to be considered available. Both fixed-host filtering and loose-host filtering call this predicate with the user's overrides and busy intervals, so occupied hosts can be offered. An override should replace normal working hours, not calendar conflicts: skip the normal-working-hours check when an override exists, but still run the busy-interval check.

When a slot falls on a date override and passes the override checks, this returns true before busy.every runs. A host with a booking during their override hours is therefore marked available for that conflicting slot. Passing the override check must continue to the busy checks rather than establish final availability.

Each dayjs call creates a distinct object, so this strict equality is always false even when start and end represent the same instant. An override marking a day unavailable will not be rejected here and can instead reach the dateOverrideExist true return. Compare timestamps with isSame.

find returns a rejection when any interval on the weekday does not contain the slot. With split hours such as 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00, a 10:00 slot is rejected by the afternoon interval and a 14:00 slot by the morning interval. Availability should require containment in at least one interval, not containment in every interval.

The value named end repeats slotStartTime instead of measuring slotEndTime. A slot beginning before the working-hours boundary but finishing after it passes this check. Use the actual slot end for the end-boundary comparison.

The end value is calculated from slotStartTime rather than slotEndTime. For working hours 09:00–10:00, a 60-minute slot starting at 09:30 passes this check even though it ends at 10:30. This matters when aggregate slots are checked against each host's individual availability. Compare the actual slot end against the working-hours end.

These comparisons reject only slots outside the override rather than requiring the entire slot to fit. With a 09:00–10:00 override, both 08:30–09:30 and 09:30–10:30 pass and reach the dateOverrideExist return true; a slot starting exactly at 10:00 also passes. When validating a host against aggregate slots, this can mark them available outside their override. Reject when the slot starts before the override start or ends after its end.

issues.descricao: The working-hours check computes end from slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime, so slots that start within working hours but end after them are accepted.
issues.textoGolden: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `end` is computed as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` — an exact duplicate of `start` — instead of using `slotEndTime`. WHY: the working-hours upper-bound test `end > workingHour.endTime` therefore compares the slot START against the working-day end, so a slot whose start is inside working hours but whose end (start + eventLength) overruns `workingHour.endTime` is never filtered and is reported as available, allowing bookings outside the host's working hours. HOW: compute `const end = slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute();`.

`end` is computed from `slotStartTime` instead of `slotEndTime`, so it always equals `start`. The `end > workingHour.endTime` check is identical to the `start` check and never catches a slot that starts within working hours but ends past them. Use `slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute()` for `end`.

`end` is computed identically to `start` (both from slotStartTime), so the check `start < workingHour.startTime || end > workingHour.endTime` can never reject a slot on the upper bound. A slot starting inside working hours but ending after workingHour.endTime is wrongly considered available; derive `end` from slotEndTime instead.

issues.descricao: The date-override check compares two dayjs objects with ===, which is always false, so zero-length (day off) overrides are never detected.
issues.textoGolden: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

comentarios.texto: This compares two separately constructed dayjs objects with `===` (reference equality), which is always false, so a zero-length override (start equal to end, whole day blocked) never returns true here. Compare timestamps, e.g. `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes'))`.

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` compares two separate dayjs object references, so `===` is always false. The zero-length date-override branch is dead code and such an override is never recognised as covering the day; compare values (e.g. .isSame() or .valueOf() === .valueOf()) instead.

The equality check compares two separately created Dayjs objects with ===, which is always false, even when the override start and end represent the same instant. The intended zero-length/closed-day rejection is unreachable, and a slot beginning exactly at that instant can reach the dateOverrideExist success return. Compare timestamps or use isSame instead.

issues.descricao: When a date override exists for the day, checkIfIsAvailable returns true before checking busy times, so slots overlapping existing bookings are reported available.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: when `dateOverrideExist` is true the function returns `true` before running the `busy.every(...)` check at the end. WHY: on any day that has a matching date override, a slot inside the override is reported available without checking the host's existing bookings (`busy` is spread via `...schedule`/`...userSchedule`), so a fixed/loose host who already has a booking during the override window is still shown as free — enabling double-booking. HOW: do not return early here; fall through so the override branch only decides whether the slot is inside the override window, and let the existing `busy` evaluation decide availability (e.g. `if (dateOverrideExist) { /* within override, still check busy */ } else { /* fall through to busy */ }`).

The new `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;` short-circuits the `busy` conflict check (and the workingHours check) for any slot that falls inside a date override window. Every caller of `checkIfIsAvailable` previously counted on it returning false for a slot that overlaps an existing booking; on days covered by a date override that guarantee is gone, so slots conflicting with the user's real bookings are now reported as available and can be double-booked. The override branch should let control fall through to the `busy.every(...)` check (returning true only for the availability-window part) instead of returning early.

A matching date override returns true before checking busy periods. Both fixed-host and loose-host callers pass calendar and booking conflicts in busy, so a host with an override is offered even when an existing booking overlaps the slot. Continue to the busy checks after validating the override instead of returning true.

issues.descricao: The working-hours check rejects a slot when any interval for the weekday excludes it, so split schedules (e.g. morning and afternoon) reject all slots.

comentarios.texto: The working-hours predicate rejects a slot if any interval on its weekday does not contain it. A split schedule of 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00 therefore loses every slot, since each valid slot lies outside the other interval. Require at least one matching interval to contain the full event instead of finding an interval that excludes it.

This search rejects a slot if it falls outside any working-hours window on that weekday. With split hours of 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00, a valid 10:00 slot is rejected because it is outside the afternoon window. Check for containment in at least one applicable window rather than finding any window that excludes the slot.

WHAT: Outside-working-hours test uses workingHours.find() returning true if ANY entry rejects the slot. WHY: With split schedules (two entries same weekday, e.g. morning+afternoon) a valid morning slot is outside the afternoon entry, find() matches and the slot is wrongly rejected as outside hours. HOW: Invert logic to accept if ANY entry contains the slot (e.g. !workingHours.some(entry contains slot) => outside).

issues.descricao: The date-override bound compares the slot start, not the slot end, with the override end, so slots extending past the override are accepted.

comentarios.texto: The override bounds reject only non-overlapping slots rather than requiring the entire event to fit inside an override. A fixed host with a 10:00–11:00 override accepts a 10:30–11:30 event generated from another host's availability, despite being unavailable for its final half hour. Accept only when at least one override contains both slotStartTime and slotEndTime; this also avoids rejecting a slot merely because another interval on the same date does not overlap it.

The upper bound checks whether slotStartTime is after the override end. A slot that starts before the override end but finishes after it is treated as available. Compare slotEndTime with the override end using isAfter, so the slot must fit entirely inside the override.

issues.descricao: The override timezone conversion keeps only hour and minute, so overrides that cross midnight in the invitee timezone become inverted ranges or are applied to the wrong day.

comentarios.texto: Timezone conversion takes only hour and minute, discarding day rollover and turning intervals crossing attendee midnight into reversed ranges. A UTC organizer's 22:00–23:00 override viewed in UTC+01:30 becomes startTime 1410 and endTime 30, which buildSlots skips because start is greater than end, removing valid availability. Preserve the converted dates and split the interval across attendee-day boundaries before building slots.

WHAT: activeOverrides are filtered by UTC day (line 206-207) before the invitee/organizer offset is applied (lines 212-224), and shifted hours are not re-bucketed across midnight. WHY: An override that shifts to the previous/next calendar day in the invitee timezone is dropped from the wrong day or applied to the wrong day, so slots show open when the organizer is off (and vice versa). HOW: Filter/bucket overrides in the invitee-local date after applying the offset, or emit split entries spanning two invitee days.

issues.descricao: The new working-hours check does not reject slots on weekdays that have no working-hours entry, so those slots are treated as available.

comentarios.texto: A weekday with no matching working-hours entry falls through to the busy checks and is treated as available when there are no conflicts. In round-robin events, slots generated for a loose host can consequently include a fixed host whose schedule excludes that day. Reject slots unless a working-hours interval on the slot's weekday contains the event, when no date override applies.

issues.descricao: Claims checkIfIsAvailable interprets date overrides in organizerTimeZone instead of each override owner's timezone.

comentarios.texto: checkIfIsAvailable interprets date overrides in the wrong timezone: the producer (slots.ts:411-415) attaches `timeZone` (the override owner's tz) to each date override and packages/lib/slots.ts:211-225 consumes `override.timeZone` to place the override window; but here `dateOverrides` is typed/used without `timeZone` and the offset is derived from the function-level `organizerTimeZone` (`dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).utcOffset() * -1`). When an override's owner timezone differs from `organizerTimeZone`, the day grid this validator uses to accept/reject a slot differs from the grid getSlots used to generate it, so generated override slots get incorrectly filtered (and the `* -1` sign is opposite to lib's `invitee - organizer`). Use the per-override `date.timeZone` (as lib does) so both files agree on which timezone defines an override.

sugestoes.texto: The async forEach callback turns getCalendar failures into rejected promises that the surrounding try/catch cannot catch. Invalid encrypted CalDAV/Apple credentials can throw during service construction (packages/lib/CalendarService.ts decrypts and JSON-parses the key), so rescheduling now produces an unhandled rejection instead of logging the error and continuing; the same regression appears in wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts. Await Promise.all over mapped callbacks inside the try block, or use an awaited for...of loop, in both implementations.

The enclosing forEach does not await its async callbacks. Previously getCalendar returned synchronously, so callbacks could populate apiDeletes before yielding; this new await yields before any calendar operations are queued. The handler can consequently await the current apiDeletes array and finish without waiting for recurring calendar updates/deletions, allowing failures to escape the cancellation flow and work to be lost when the request ends. Await the credential callbacks (for example with Promise.all over map), or use an awaited for...of loop, before consuming apiDeletes.

This async forEach is not awaited. Adding await getCalendar here means each callback now suspends before it can register the recurring-event operations in apiDeletes. The handler can reach its Promise.all(apiDeletes) and finish cancellation before those operations have been added, leaving external recurring events stale (and subsequent failures outside the handler's awaited work). Await the iteration itself, for example with an awaited Promise.all over map, before consuming apiDeletes.

issues.descricao: Async callbacks passed to forEach after getCalendar became async are never awaited, so calendar and video cancellations run fire-and-forget, may not finish, and their errors escape the surrounding try/catch as unhandled rejections.
issues.textoGolden: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

comentarios.texto: The async forEach callback moves calendar factory exceptions outside the surrounding try/catch because forEach discards its returned promise. An invalid encrypted Exchange credential throws during CalendarService construction, now producing an unhandled rejection while Reschedule continues and returns success instead of logging the error; the identical regression occurs in wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts. Await Promise.all over bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...) inside the try block, or use an awaited for...of loop, so factory and deletion failures reach the catch.

The new async forEach callback is not awaited. If getCalendar rejects (for example, the dynamically imported calendar module fails to load or its service constructor throws), the callback produces a rejected promise that forEach discards; the surrounding try/catch cannot catch it. Previously a synchronous getCalendar failure reached that catch. Await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...)) or use an awaited for...of loop so these failures remain handled and calendar cleanup completes before rescheduling continues. Apply the same fix to the equivalent changed loop in wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts.

WHAT: credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { await getCalendar; apiDeletes.push(...) }) pushes to apiDeletes asynchronously after outer code consumes it. WHY: outer apiDeletes is awaited elsewhere while async callbacks have not yet pushed, so recurring-event deletions are lost/partial and errors are unobserved. HOW: replace with for...of with await or collect promises via map + await Promise.all.

issues.descricao: Suggests wrapping the awaited dynamic app import in try-catch to handle import failures, without identifying a defect.
issues.textoGolden: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

issues.descricao: Claims consumers of getCalendarCredentials call methods on or null-check an un-awaited Promise; every consumer goes through getConnectedCalendars, which awaits it.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: getCalendar changed to async Promise<Calendar|null> but packages/core/CalendarManager.ts getCalendarCredentials still does const calendar = getCalendar(credential) synchronously without await. WHY: every entry now stores a Promise instead of Calendar, so any consumer not patched to await item.calendar (e.g. callers in viewer.tsx/calendar.ts paths) sees a truthy Promise, breaks null checks and calls listCalendars/createEvent on wrong type. HOW: make getCalendarCredentials async and await getCalendar, updating its callers.
