sugestoes.texto: Targets are now template-interpolated here and then interpolated again by DataSourceWithBackend.query (line 185) when runQuery calls super.query. A variable whose literal value contains another defined variable token, such as `$other` in a log search string, is substituted a second time and sends different query text than the user selected; shard splitting adds another pass through its own new mapping before reaching this function. Preserve the early interpolation needed for splitting, but ensure already-interpolated targets are not interpolated again during execution.

issues.descricao: Loki split/shard queries are now interpolated with applyTemplateVariables before splitting and again on execution, so ad hoc filters are applied twice and already-substituted values are re-interpolated.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: runShardSplitQuery now interpolates every target via datasource.applyTemplateVariables (line 52), but it then delegates each sub-request to runSplitQuery (line 163), which this PR also changed to call datasource.applyTemplateVariables again (querySplitting.ts:299), so each target is interpolated (and ad hoc filters applied) twice. WHY: double interpolation re-runs addAdHocFilters on an already-filtered expression; the stream-selector path masks the duplicate via labelExists() dedup in addFilterToStreamSelector (modifyQuery.ts:494), but parsed/structured-metadata labels use addFilterAsLabelFilter which does not dedup, producing duplicated label filters, and any interpolated value containing '$' can be re-interpolated. This is confirmed by the updated test expecting applyTemplateVariables toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5) for a single target (1 call here + 4 sub-requests through runSplitQuery) instead of 1. HOW: interpolate only once — either remove the interpolation added to runShardSplitQuery and let runSplitQuery do it, or have splitQueriesByStreamShard pass the already-interpolated targets without re-interpolating in runSplitQuery.

The newly interpolated targets are interpolated again by DataSourceWithBackend.query when runQuery executes each split request. TemplateSrv.replace scans the resulting string again, so a variable whose literal value contains another defined variable token (for example, a log-search value containing `$other`) is expanded a second time and produces a different query from the non-splitting path; shard splitting also passes through this additional interpolation. Preserve the early interpolation needed for partitioning while ensuring already-interpolated targets are not interpolated again on execution, and test through the real backend query preparation rather than mocking runQuery.

Targets are interpolated here with `applyTemplateVariables`, including ad hoc filters, and then sent to `datasource.runQuery`, which interpolates them again through the backend path (datasource.ts:324/377). The ad hoc filters may be injected twice, and already-substituted values are re-interpolated, which can produce wrong or invalid LogQL. Interpolate only once. Either clear `scopedVars` and `filters` on the sub-requests after the first pass, or skip interpolation in `runQuery` for already-interpolated requests. The same issue applies to shardQuerySplitting.ts:52.

issues.descricao: runShardSplitQuery now filters empty/hidden targets before interpolation, so an expr that interpolates to an empty string is no longer dropped.

comentarios.texto: The order of operations was inverted relative to the previous contract: interpolation used to run before the `expr`/`hide` filters (interpolateVariablesInQueries(targets).filter(...)), and now the filters run on the *raw* targets before `applyTemplateVariables` is applied. Filtering on the un-interpolated `query.expr` means the previous fallback that dropped a target once variable substitution had emptied its expression no longer exists: a target like `{ expr: '$myVar' }` whose variable resolves to '' is truthy at filter time, survives, is then interpolated to `''`, and is passed into the shard splitting/execution loop as a blank query. To preserve the old contract the filters should run on the interpolated result (or the interpolated expr should be re-checked for emptiness).

issues.descricao: Claims interpolating before partitioning substitutes $__range so range queries are wrongly split; applyTemplateVariables leaves $__range untouched.

comentarios.texto: Interpolating (line 299) before the splitting partition (line 300) breaks the `$__range` guard. `querySupportsSplitting`/`isQueryWithRangeVariable` deliberately keeps queries with `$__range` out of splitting because that variable is interpolated against the split time range and would be wrong (see the comment at lines 285-287). applyTemplateVariables/templateSrv.replace substitutes built-in variables like `$__range`/`$__interval`/`$__auto`, so by the time `partition(... !querySupportsSplitting(query))` runs the expression no longer contains `$__range`, the guard returns false, and such queries are now split — producing range-windowed results computed against each chunk instead of the whole query range. Keep the range-variable check on the un-interpolated expression: run the partition/querySupportsSplitting test on the raw targets (or capture the raw expr before mapping) and only interpolate the queries that actually go to execution.

Interpolating the targets here (via applyTemplateVariables) happens before the partition that calls querySupportsSplitting(), so its `!isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` guard now inspects the already-interpolated expression. $__range is resolved by the frontend templateSrv.replace used inside applyTemplateVariables, so the raw `$__range` token the guard looks for is gone by the time the guard runs, and queries using $__range are no longer excluded from splitting. Per the comment right above (lines 285-286), those queries must not be split because the $__range interpolation uses the split time range and yields incorrect results. Preserve the range-variable check against the original, un-interpolated expr (e.g. run querySupportsSplitting on request.targets, or evaluate isQueryWithRangeVariable before applying applyTemplateVariables).

issues.descricao: Notes test coverage of the new interpolation; no issue.

comentarios.texto: The `.map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters))` is correctly covered by the new test. If removed, the expr reaching runQuery would retain `$__auto` and step would remain `$step`.

issues.descricao: Notes test coverage of shard interpolation; no issue.

comentarios.texto: Interpolation in `runShardSplitQuery` is covered by the new test, which uses a real datasource. If `applyTemplateVariables` were not applied, `$__auto`/`$step` would survive.

issues.descricao: The interpolation test hardcodes the number of applyTemplateVariables calls, making it brittle to unrelated splitting changes.

comentarios.texto: The `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` assertion in the new interpolation tests is brittle because it hardcodes the number of split requests. It still fails if interpolation is dropped, but it may break on unrelated changes to the splitting logic. Consider asserting on the interpolated expr/step instead of, or in addition to, the exact call count.

issues.descricao: The new interpolation tests do not set request.filters, so passing ad hoc filters to applyTemplateVariables is untested.
issues.textoGolden: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

sugestoes.texto: This helper returns false for both values of FlagSqlExpressions. Consequently the new guard rejects every SQL expression, including when the feature is explicitly enabled. Return the actual flag value so enabled requests can reach SQL parsing.

The parser and SQL command now use this DB instead of the working DuckDB implementation, but RunCommands and QueryFramesInto unconditionally return errors. Thus table discovery and query execution cannot succeed even after the feature gate is corrected (or for direct callers). Preserve the functional backend until this replacement implements those operations.

The local backend is not behaviorally compatible with the DuckDB backend it replaces: RunCommands and QueryFramesInto unconditionally fail. sql.TablesList still calls RunCommands and propagates its error, so NewSQLCommand now rejects every nonempty valid query as invalid; SQLCommand.Execute likewise cannot produce a frame. The new reader gate does not cover the other NewSQLCommand caller confirmed in sql_command.go. Preserve the working backend until the replacement implements these operations, or explicitly update all consumers to an unsupported-feature contract rather than routing valid SQL through an always-failing implementation.

issues.descricao: The variable in TablesList is still named duckDB although it no longer holds a DuckDB instance.

comentarios.texto: After replacing `duck.NewInMemoryDB()` with local `NewInMemoryDB()` and removing the duck import, the local `duckDB` still carries the old implementation name though it is no longer a duck DB. Rename to `db`/`sqlDB` (as done in sql_command.go) so identifier matches code.

issues.descricao: enableSqlExpressions always returns false regardless of the sqlExpressions feature flag, so SQL expressions are rejected unconditionally.
issues.textoGolden: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:

comentarios.texto: WHAT: enableSqlExpressions always returns false regardless of the feature flag — the computed `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` value is never returned (both `if enabled { return false }` and the trailing `return false` yield false). WHY: the `sqlExpressions` toggle is read but has no effect, so SQL expressions are unconditionally dead-disabled and any intent to let the flag opt the feature back in is silently broken (dead code indicating a logic mistake). HOW: return the flag state, e.g. `return h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`, with the polarization matching the intended enable/disable semantics.

`enableSqlExpressions` always returns false: the value computed on line 195 (`enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`) is never used — both the `if enabled { return false }` branch and the final `return false` return false. Consequently the QueryTypeSQL branch (reader.go:128-132) always fails with "sqlExpressions is not implemented", so the feature flag can never enable SQL expressions. Return the computed value (and drop the erroneous `!` so the flag enables rather than disables the feature).

`enableSqlExpressions` always returns false: it computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` but then returns false in both the `if enabled` branch (line 197) and the fall-through (line 199), so the flag value is never propagated. The caller at reader.go:129-132 treats a false result as 'feature off' and returns an error, so QueryTypeSQL is permanently blocked regardless of FlagSqlExpressions. Return the flag's own value (drop the `!` and the constant returns), e.g. `return h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`.

issues.descricao: The go-duck DB was replaced by a stub whose methods always return 'not implemented', so table parsing and SQL expression execution always fail.
issues.textoGolden: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: TablesList now delegates to the stub `NewInMemoryDB()`, whose `RunCommands` (pkg/expr/sql/db.go:16-18) always returns errors.New("not implemented"), so TablesList can never return tables. WHY: its callers `sql.TablesList` in NewSQLCommand (sql_command.go:30) and the SQLCommand execution path (QueryFramesInto, sql_command.go:100) now always fail with an error, permanently breaking the parser contract (and the existing parser_test.go suite that expects real table lists). HOW: if SQL is intentionally disabled, remove the now-dead parser/command paths or keep a functional parser; otherwise restore a working DB implementation.

NewInMemoryDB() returns a stub whose TablesList/RunCommands/QueryFramesInto always return errors.New("not implemented"), replacing the working go-duck in-memory DB. This makes TablesList always fail (so NewSQLCommand always errors) and QueryFramesInto always fail in SQLCommand.Execute, so every SQL expression breaks at runtime. Wire up a real implementation (restore the go-duck-backed DB) instead of a stub that always errors.

The DB type that replaces duck.NewInMemoryDB() is a stub: TablesList, RunCommands and QueryFramesInto all unconditionally return errors.New("not implemented"). Its consumers were not updated to match this new contract — parser.go:26 calls RunCommands and now always errors, so NewSQLCommand (sql_command.go:30) rejects every SQL query as invalid, and sql_command.go:100 calls QueryFramesInto and always sets rsp.Error. Either these methods must be implemented or the callers must be guarded so a not-implemented DB does not silently break the SQL expression path.

issues.descricao: Claims the rejection message says 'not implemented' though the guard is a feature-flag check.

comentarios.texto: The rejection message reads `"sqlExpressions is not implemented"`, but the guard it sits behind (`enableSqlExpressions`) tests whether the `FlagSqlExpressions` feature flag is enabled — it is a gating condition, not a missing implementation. The text tells the caller the feature does not exist rather than that it is turned off, so the message disagrees with the check that produced it; make the message describe the actual reason (the feature not being enabled).

sugestoes.texto: The denial cache key ambiguously concatenates resource name and parent folder with underscores. Valid UIDs can contain underscores, so a denial for name `a_b` in folder `c` also denies name `a` in folder `b_c`, even when the latter has an explicit permission grant, because Check returns before examining permissions. Encode the components unambiguously, for example as a JSON array, and add a collision regression test.

The unescaped underscore concatenation does not uniquely encode the request. For the same namespace, user and action, name `a_b` with parent `c` generates exactly the same key as name `a` with parent `b_c`. A cached denial for the first request then makes Check return false for the second without evaluating its permissions, even if it is allowed. Encode the components unambiguously (for example JSON or length-prefixed fields) and use a distinct denial-cache prefix rather than sharing `.perm_` with permission-map entries.

The denial-cache key is not unique for its input tuple. For example, the same namespace, user and action with name `a_b`, parent `c` produces exactly the same key as name `a`, parent `b_c`. Underscores can occur in resource UIDs. If the first check is denied, Check stores that denial and then unconditionally denies the second resource without consulting its permissions, even if access should be allowed. Encode the components unambiguously (for example as a JSON array or length-prefixed fields) before using them as a cache key.

issues.descricao: The denial cache key joins name and parent folder with underscores, so different name/parent pairs can collide and a cached denial for one resource denies another until TTL expiry.
issues.textoGolden: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

comentarios.texto: The denial cache key does not distinguish underscores inside resource and parent UIDs from its field separators. For the same namespace, user and action, (name="a_b", parent="c") and (name="a", parent="b_c") generate the same key, so denying the first request makes Check return false for the second even if its permissions explicitly allow it. Encode the components unambiguously, for example as a JSON tuple or length-prefixed fields.

The denial cache key is not injective: for the same namespace, user and action, `(name="a_b", parent="c")` and `(name="a", parent="b_c")` produce the same key. After the first request stores a denial, Check's new early cache return denies the second request without checking its permissions, even if it is allowed. Encode the components unambiguously (for example a JSON tuple or length-prefixed components) and add a test verifying that these two requests do not share a denial entry.

Make the denial-cache key encode component boundaries unambiguously (for example, length-prefix or serialize the components). For the same namespace, user and action, name `a_b` with parent `c` and name `a` with parent `b_c` both produce the suffix `_a_b_c`. Underscores can occur in resource UIDs, so denying the first request caches a key that causes Check to immediately deny the second request without evaluating its permissions, even if that resource is allowed.

issues.descricao: The explicit denial-cache test seeds the cached permission as false instead of true, so it would pass without the denial-cache short-circuit and does not verify it.
issues.textoGolden: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

comentarios.texto: This test claims to prove the permDenialCache short-circuit (service.go:116-121) denies access, but it seeds the cached permission as map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false} (a deny), contradicting its comment "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked". Because the cached set is already a deny, checkPermission returns allowed=false, the code falls through to the DB path, and the fake store also returns no permissions, so Allowed stays false. The assertion passes even if the entire permDenialCache early-return were deleted. Seed the cached permission as true (map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": true}) so that only the denial-cache entry can force Allowed=false; otherwise the test does not verify the feature.

The comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but the code sets the permCache entry to `false`, which is a deny. The test therefore does not show that the permission cache is skipped. Set the value to `true`, or change the comment to match.

The 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' test would still pass if the permDenialCache check were removed. permCache is seeded with dash1:false, not true as the comment claims, so the normal path also denies. Seed permCache with {"dashboards:uid:dash1": true} and a store that grants the permission, so Allowed=false can only come from the denial entry.

issues.descricao: A cached permission set that denies a resource always triggers a full DB permission reload, so checks over many inaccessible dashboards issue one query per resource instead of being served from cache.

comentarios.texto: Every distinct resource denied by the cached permission map triggers a reload of the entire user's action permission set, because the denial cache is resource-specific and a cached false result always falls through to getIdentityPermissions. Sequential checks of N inaccessible dashboards therefore execute N full permission queries and cache rewrites even with a current action-wide cache; getUserPermissions' singleflight only merges overlapping requests. Bound refreshes per user/action with a short refresh cooldown or generation marker so different resource misses can share a recent refresh.

issues.descricao: The Service struct comment listing its caches was not updated for the new permDenialCache field.

comentarios.texto: The struct doc comment still reads "// Cache for user permissions, user team memberships and user basic roles", but this PR added the new `permDenialCache` field (line 58). The comment no longer enumerates what the struct actually holds and misleads a reader about the new denial-cache field; update it to mention the permission-denial cache so the prose matches the fields.

issues.descricao: Claims a cached denial blocks access granted within the TTL window; denials are TTL-bounded like the existing permission cache.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The permDenialCache short-circuit (lines 116-121) runs before the newly-added requery-on-miss logic (lines 123-136), so a cached denial is returned as Allowed:false with no requery. WHY: The denial is written at line 154 only after an authoritative DB deny, but for the exact scenario this PR targets — a resource whose permission row is committed just after the deny was recorded (newly created dashboard/folder) — the stale denial is served for the whole shortCacheTTL (30s) even though the user now has access, defeating the requery fix added in the same function and producing a spurious permission-denied for newly created resources. HOW: When the denial-cache entry is hit, re-validate against fresh permissions (or skip the denial short-circuit for create/just-created resources), or invalidate the denial entry on resource creation/permission change instead of relying only on TTL.

Check now consults permDenialCache first and returns Allowed:false without consulting the store. Previously a Check whose permission-cache lookup missed or evaluated to not-allowed always fell back to getIdentityPermissions (the store) before it could refuse, so a false result reflected current store state. Now every denial is memoized (service.go 153-155) and identical subsequent requests (same namespace/userUID/action/name/parent) are refused from cache for the whole shortCacheTTL, so a permission granted after the denial was cached is still refused. If the denial short-circuit is intended, make the contract explicit (document the TTL staleness) and ensure denial entries are invalidated on permission changes; otherwise remove the unconditional deny short-circuit or gate it so a fresh evaluation is still possible.

A denial cached for shortCacheTTL is returned before the permission cache is checked or refreshed. A user who is granted access within that window (for example, after creating the dashboard or folder) keeps getting denied until the entry expires, which is the case this PR is meant to fix. Invalidate the denial entry when permissions are refreshed or granted, or use a much shorter TTL for denial entries.

issues.descricao: Claims trusting cached grants while re-checking cached denials lets stale grants keep access to revoked resources; cached grants were already served for the TTL before this PR.
issues.textoGolden: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

issues.descricao: Claims per-resource denial entries cause unbounded cache memory growth; entries expire after the short TTL.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: every denied Check inserts a per-resource denial entry keyed by (namespace,user,action,name,parent). WHY: cache cardinality explodes from O(users x actions) to O(users x actions x resources), causing unbounded memory growth and eviction pressure on the shared local cache as dashboard/folder counts grow.

issues.descricao: Claims List now serves stale cached permissions whereas it previously always queried the DB; List was already cache-backed before the change.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: List serves listPermission directly from getCachedIdentityPermissions on any cache hit with no outdated-cache requery, unlike Check which falls through to the DB when cached perms deny. WHY: newly granted dashboard/folder scopes missing from the cached map stay missing from List results for the full TTL, while pre-PR List always hit the DB via getIdentityPermissions.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: The SQLite fallback reconstructs the complete accumulated ID list with fmt.Sprintf on every iteration. WHY: Building a batch of N IDs copies O(N²) characters; the newly supported 32,767-ID batches allocate gigabytes of temporary strings across construction, adding GC pressure and delaying cleanup on the shared server. HOW: Build the comma-separated list with strings.Builder and append each formatted ID once.

WHAT: The ticker interval changes from ten minutes to one minute for the entire cleanup service. WHY: Every tick calls clean(), which runs all eight jobs, including dashboard-version, snapshot, image, and query-history cleanup, so this annotation-query change also increases unrelated recurring cleanup work tenfold on every instance. HOW: Preserve the ten-minute interval; if annotations require a different cadence, schedule that job separately.

This case never actually deletes a batch exceeding the SQLite >= 3.32.0 parameter limit it names. createTestAnnotations distributes the 40,003 annotations among three types, and CleanAnnotations fetches/deletes each type separately, so each DELETE receives only about 13,334 IDs despite the configured batch size of 32,767. Removing the SQLite literal-ID workaround would therefore still pass this regression test on those SQLite versions. Create more than 32,766 deletable annotations of a single type (or enough total annotations that one type exceeds that threshold), and update the expected counts accordingly.

issues.descricao: Leftover debug logs in the annotation cleanup emit Error-level entries with the full ID list on every batch, flooding error logs during normal operation.
issues.textoGolden: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Leftover debug logging calls r.log.Error on every cleanup batch (also duplicated at lines 554-557 and 576-579) dumping full ids slice, cond, and nil err at Error level. WHY: Fires Error-level log per batch and serializes up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize IDs (32767 in new test), spamming error logs/monitoring on every normal cleanup run. HOW: Downgrade to Debug or remove; do not log full ids at Error.

WHAT: Leftover debug logging calls `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, ...)` (and the identical Error-level logs for 'by count' and 'Tags to clean', lines 554/557/576/579) run on every batch in production. WHY: These log the full ID slice (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize, e.g. 32767 elements) at Error severity on every cleanup iteration, flooding logs with false error noise and large payloads for a normal successful operation, and can trigger error-based alerting. HOW: Remove these log lines, or downgrade to Debug and drop the full `ids` slice (log only the count).

Avoid using Error-level logging on the normal cleanup path. The new r.log.Error calls emit count, ids, cond, and err at lines 534/537, 554/557, and 576/579 during non-error execution, creating log noise; consider downgrading or removing these logs on the normal path.

issues.descricao: The comment states SQLite's parameter limit is 999, which is only true for SQLite versions before 3.32.0.

comentarios.texto: The comment states that SQLite has a parameter limit of 999, but SQLite >= 3.32.0 defaults to 32766 (as the added integration test also recognizes). This branch is choosing a conservative compatibility threshold, not expressing the limit of every SQLite database. Document 999 as the older-version/compatibility threshold so maintainers do not mistake this constant for the actual limit on modern SQLite.

issues.descricao: On MySQL and Postgres, deleteByIDs binds one placeholder per ID without limit, so a cleanup batch size above 65535 makes every DELETE fail.

comentarios.texto: The bind-parameter workaround only handles SQLite's limit; the placeholder branch is used for every other engine with len(ids) placeholders and no bound. The previous implementation had no bind parameters, so this path is new. Postgres (extended protocol) and MySQL both cap bind parameters at 65535, so a configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize larger than that makes this DELETE fail at Exec with a parameter-limit error instead of cleaning anything. Clamp the number of ids per DELETE (e.g. chunk into <=1000/<=65535 id sub-batches) for all dialects, not just SQLite.

On Postgres and MySQL, deleteByIDs binds one placeholder per ID with no cap. A configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above the driver's bind-parameter limit (65535) makes every cleanup batch fail, and the cleanup job then never finishes. Split the IDs into chunks below the limit, or inline the integer IDs as the SQLite branch does.

issues.descricao: The SQLite inline ID list is built with repeated fmt.Sprintf concatenation, which is quadratic in batch size.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: SQLite large-batch IN-list built with repeated fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) in a loop over ids. WHY: Quadratic string copying on large batches (e.g. 32767 IDs in added test) during cleanup, a background job path. HOW: Build with strings.Builder or strings.Join.

The SQLite literal-ID path rebuilds the entire accumulated string for every ID, making SQL construction quadratic in batch size. Large batches explicitly supported by this PR, including the 32,767 setting in the integration test, generate substantial repeated copying and allocation before each delete, consuming cleanup time and memory. Build the list with strings.Builder and append each formatted ID once.

issues.descricao: The cleanup service ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, running every cleanup job ten times as often and increasing database load.
issues.textoGolden: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute with no justification. WHY: Runs all 8 cleanup jobs including the new multi-query (SELECT+DELETE per batch) annotation cleanup 10x more often, multiplying DB load. HOW: Revert to 10 minutes or justify the frequency change separately.

WHAT: The cleanup job ticker interval was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. WHY: This runs all cleanup jobs (annotations, expired snapshots/versions/images, short URLs, query history) 10× more frequently, multiplying background DB load and lock contention — the opposite of the deadlock mitigation this PR targets — and appears to be a debug leftover unrelated to the described change. HOW: Restore the ticker to `time.Minute * 10`.

The cleanup ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`, a 10x increase in how often the entire cleanup job runs. This job also drives the annotation/tag cleanup path changed in this PR, which now fetches ID batches into memory and emits Error-level logs per batch, so running it every minute substantially increases DB load and log volume with no functional benefit. Unless a 1-minute cadence is explicitly intended, this should stay at 10 minutes (it reads like a leftover from testing).

issues.descricao: Empty comment with no claim.
Garbled text on the cleanup ticker line with no identifiable claim.

comentarios.texto: 删除了this later

issues.descricao: Claims the SQLite-limit regression test never sends more than 32,766 parameters to an annotation DELETE because the fixtures are split across three types.

comentarios.texto: The new SQLite-limit regression case does not exceed the parameter limit when deleting annotations. The 40,003 fixtures are distributed across alert, dashboard and API types, and CleanAnnotations selects/deletes each type separately, so each annotation DELETE receives only about 13,333 IDs despite the configured batch size of 32,767. On SQLite >=3.32.0, switching annotation deletion back to placeholders would therefore still pass this test (the tag cleanup can independently retain its workaround). Create more than 32,767 annotations of a single type, or enough total fixtures for at least one type's deletion to exceed 32,766 parameters, and assert that cleanup succeeds.

sugestoes.texto: The registered fallback provider throws UnsupportedOperationException when constructing EC parameters required by AbstractJWKParser. With authz-client as the only crypto provider, AuthzClient.create now installs this provider globally, so parsing a P-256, P-384, or P-521 JWK fails before ECDSA signature verification can run; AbstractJWKParser also requires getKeyFactory("ECDSA"), which this provider rejects. Implement EC parameter construction and EC key-factory lookup using the JDK APIs so the fallback supports the EC JWK parsing path.

readSequence accepts child encodings that extend past the sequence's declared content length. For example, 30 05 02 01 01 02 01 01 is accepted as two integers even though the second integer extends outside the five-byte sequence, and asn1derToConcatenatedRS consequently converts a malformed DER signature instead of rejecting it. Reject a child whose encoded length exceeds the remaining sequence length and require the remaining length to reach exactly zero.

The loop accepts a child whose encoded length exceeds the remaining sequence content: subtraction makes length negative and the method returns successfully. For example, `30 04 02 01 01 02 01 01` declares four content bytes but contains two three-byte INTEGERs; readSequence returns both, and asn1derToConcatenatedRS accepts the malformed signature. Require each child to fit within the remaining sequence length (and reject a negative remainder), so bytes outside the declared sequence cannot become its members.

Reject a child whose encoded size exceeds the sequence's remaining content length. Currently, for example, `30 01 02 01 01` is accepted: the sequence declares one content byte, but readNext consumes the entire three-byte INTEGER, then length becomes -2 and the loop returns successfully. A sequence containing two integers can likewise be accepted with its declared length ending inside the second integer. This lets malformed signatures cross the enclosing ASN.1 boundary instead of producing an IOException.

Both sides of the assertion originate from the decoder under test. If asn1derToConcatenatedRS regressed to returning a zero-filled array of signLength, every test would still pass: encoding those zeros and decoding them again produces the same zeros. Assert that the reconstructed DER equals the original JCA DER signature, or verify the reconstructed signature against data and the public key, so lost or corrupted R/S values fail.

All three cases generate a default EC key (normally P-256); changing the signature hash to ES384/ES512 does not change the key's curve or the R/S sizes. Consequently testES512 still passes if long-form DER sequence length handling is broken, because its actual signature remains a short P-256 sequence, merely padded during conversion. Generate the matching P-256, P-384, or P-521 key inside the parameterized helper so each named case exercises its intended signature sizes.

The loop accepts a child even when its full encoding exceeds the remaining sequence length, then exits with a negative length and returns success. For example, `30 01 02 01 01` declares one content byte but returns the three-byte INTEGER as a valid sequence element. This makes the decoder return values that are not contained in the declared ASN.1 sequence. Reject an element whose encoded length exceeds the remaining content length.

All three tests generate the same default EC key (typically P-256). Selecting SHA384withECDSA or SHA512withECDSA changes the digest, not the key's curve, so the ES384 and ES512 cases merely pad P-256 components and never test real P-384/P-521 signatures. In particular, this misses the long-form DER sequence length encountered with P-521. Generate a key with an explicit curve corresponding to the algorithm inside test().

issues.descricao: concatenatedRSToASN1DER encodes r and s into two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances before re-encoding them in the return statement.
issues.textoGolden: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.

comentarios.texto: Dead computation: the two ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) calls allocate encoders and encode rBigInteger/sBigInteger, but their results are discarded — the returned DER comes entirely from the expression at lines 117-121, which re-encodes the same BigIntegers. These two statements have no effect and should be removed (they are a leftover from an earlier formulation).

Remove these two discarded encoder writes. Each allocates an encoder and encodes a BigInteger, but neither result participates in the returned signature; lines 119–120 repeat both writes on fresh encoders. This performs redundant encoding and allocations on every concatenated-signature conversion.

The two statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` encode values and discard the results. The return expression re-encodes the same values, so these lines are dead computation left over from a copy-paste or refactor. Remove them.

issues.descricao: order() is added to CryptoProvider as an abstract method, breaking source and binary compatibility for existing third-party CryptoProvider implementations.
issues.textoGolden: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations

comentarios.texto: order() was added as an abstract method to the public CryptoProvider interface. CryptoIntegration.detectProvider now invokes order() on every ServiceLoader-discovered CryptoProvider via Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order). Any CryptoProvider implementation compiled against the previous interface (an external or separately built provider jar on the classpath) will throw AbstractMethodError at detection time, i.e. during AuthzClient.create()/server bootstrap, before any provider is usable. Giving order() a default implementation (e.g. default int order() { return 0; }) avoids the binary-incompatibility.

issues.descricao: detectProvider no longer fails when several crypto providers are present; with Default, FIPS and Elytron all at order 200, ties are resolved by classpath order and a FIPS deployment can silently run with the non-FIPS provider.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: detectProvider sorts by order() reversed and silently picks index 0, removing the previous multiple-providers error. WHY: Default/FIPS/Elytron all return order 200, so ambiguous classpath (e.g. default+FIPS) now nondeterministically picks one by ServiceLoader order instead of failing fast, risking wrong FIPS vs non-FIPS crypto. HOW: only auto-ignore lower-order providers; throw when the top two have equal order().

Reject ambiguous highest-priority providers rather than silently taking the first. Both DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider return order 200 in this PR, so when both are present the stable sort leaves the decision to ServiceLoader discovery order. A deployment expecting FIPS can therefore initialize the ordinary Bouncy Castle provider without an error; previously this mixed classpath failed closed. Preserve the error for tied highest-priority providers (or require an explicit security-mode/provider choice), while still allowing the lower-priority authz-client fallback.

detectProvider() no longer fails fast when multiple CryptoProviders are present and instead silently picks the first after sorting by order() descending. All Keycloak providers return the same order (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider all return 200), so a tie between two providers is broken by the non-deterministic ServiceLoader iteration order rather than the intended priority. The previous code threw an IllegalStateException forcing the classpath to be corrected; now a deployment with two provider jars (exactly the 'multiple providers on classpath' scenario this PR enables) can silently select the unintended provider — e.g. a non-FIPS/strict provider when FIPS is required — with no error. Use a stable tie-breaker (delegate to the provider name/type) or reject equal top orders instead of relying on ServiceLoader order.

issues.descricao: Claims a wrong-length JOSE signature causes an unchecked exception in concatenatedRSToASN1DER; verifiers catch it and report verification failure, as with the existing providers.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: concatenatedRSToASN1DER splits signature without validating signature.length==signLength. WHY: short JOSE input throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and long input is silently truncated to signLength, breaking the ECDSACryptoProvider contract (IOException on malformed) used by verifier contexts. HOW: check length upfront and throw IOException.

concatenatedRSToASN1DER never validates signature.length == signLength before System.arraycopy(signature,0,r,1,len) / (signature,len,s,1,len). A short JWS signature throws unchecked ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of the declared IOException, breaking verification on attacker-controlled input. Validate length and throw IOException.

issues.descricao: The ES384 and ES512 tests sign with the same default P-256 key, so the converter is never tested with real P-384 or P-521 signatures.

comentarios.texto: Single default EC keypair reused for ES256/ES384/ES512: testES384/testES512 names claim larger curves but body signs with the same P-256 key and only pads to larger signLength, so full-width 384/521-bit handling is never exercised. Generate a per-algorithm keypair with the correct curve (e.g. secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) before signing.

Every case generates a default EC key rather than a key on the curve associated with the named algorithm. On the standard JDK this is P-256, so testES384 and testES512 just pad P-256 signature components to larger lengths. A converter that discards nonzero high bytes beyond 32 bytes would still pass all three cases. Initialize the key generator with the appropriate curve per case (P-256, P-384, and P-521) so the larger-component conversions are actually tested.

Generate a key on the curve corresponding to each tested algorithm rather than using the provider's default EC curve for all three tests. On the standard JDK this generates a P-256 key even for testES384 and testES512, so those tests merely pad P-256 integers to larger output lengths and never exercise actual P-384/P-521 signature encoding (including P-521's long-form sequence length).

issues.descricao: The test only checks a round trip between the two new converters and never verifies the re-encoded DER against the original signature or with Signature.verify, so mutually consistent bugs go undetected.

comentarios.texto: Tautological round-trip assertion: rsConcat2 is derived from rsConcat via encode+decode that are inverses if self-consistent, so assertArrayEquals(rsConcat,rsConcat2) passes even if both directions are wrong. Verify against external oracle: Signature.initVerify + verify(asn1Des) and/or compare rsConcat to expected split, not just to itself.

The test only checks self-consistency: it asserts asn1derToConcatenatedRS(g(asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign))) == asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign), i.e. that concatenatedRSToASN1DER is a right inverse of asn1derToConcatenatedRS. It never compares against the original DER `sign`, never verifies the ECDSA signature, and never asserts the emvider output is canonical DER. Because the decoder it reads back with (ASN1Decoder.readLength) accepts non-canonical long-form lengths (e.g. 0x81) and validates only tag numbers, a regression in ASN1Encoder.writeLength that always emitted long form would still round-trip and the test would still pass, even though the produced signature would no longer be valid DER and would be rejected by the Keycloak server / a JDK Signature.verify. Assert the encoded signature is valid DER (e.g. verify it with a JDK Signature, or compare asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign) against a known-good width-padded r||s and assert its length equals algorithm.getSignatureLength()).

The assertion only establishes agreement between the two new conversion routines, not correctness of the converted signature. For example, swapping r and s in both routines makes this entire round trip pass, although the DER result no longer verifies the signed data. Verify `asn1Des` with the public key and original data (or compare against an independently specified encoding) so mutually compensating conversion defects fail the test.

issues.descricao: Claims getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider instead of BouncyCastle; that is the intended fallback for the BC-free authz client.
issues.textoGolden: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)

comentarios.texto: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JVM default KeyStore provider (e.g. SUN) instead of a BouncyCastle provider, violating the method's contract ('@return BouncyCastle security provider'). This value is consumed by BouncyIntegration.loadProvider() (common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/util/BouncyIntegration.java:34) to set the static BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER name, so whenever this authz-client provider is the one selected by CryptoIntegration, every Keycloak code path that does getInstance(..., BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER) silently looks algorithms up in a non-BC provider (e.g. 'SUN'), which can produce failures or different crypto implementation than expected. Returning a provider that is not BouncyCastle while claiming to be the BouncyCastle provider makes BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER point to the wrong provider.

getBouncyCastleProvider() returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), i.e. the JDK default keystore provider (SUN), yet the method name and the CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() contract say it returns the BouncyCastle provider. A caller that uses the returned Provider as the BouncyCastle provider (to look up BC algorithms or to register it) will silently get the wrong (often already-registered) provider. Either return the actual BC provider or rename/document the method so the name matches what it returns.

WHAT: getBouncyCastleProvider returns KeyStore.getInstance(defaultType).getProvider() (e.g. SUN) as the BouncyCastle provider. WHY: BouncyIntegration.loadProvider caches this name for all Signature/Cipher/KeyFactory lookups, so standalone authz-client gets PROVIDER=SUN instead of BC/null and BC-specific algorithms/FIPS expectations break. HOW: return null like WildFlyElytronProvider does when no BC provider is available.

issues.descricao: Claims readLength's -1 for indefinite-length encoding breaks length arithmetic or array allocation; the decoder only parses locally generated DER and the sequence path already rejects it.
issues.textoGolden: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: readLength returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding 0x80 and callers pass it to new byte[length]. WHY: causes NegativeArraySizeException (unchecked) in readInteger/readNext instead of IOException, crashing signature-verification callers that expect checked failure on malformed DER. HOW: throw IOException for 0x80 since DER forbids indefinite lengths.

readInteger passes readLength() result directly to read(length)->new byte[length]. readLength returns -1 for indefinite-length 0x80, so a crafted INTEGER with length 0x80 throws unchecked NegativeArraySizeException at allocation instead of IOException. Reject length<0 here (indefinite length not valid for DER INTEGER).

readInteger() calls readLength(), which returns -1 for an indefinite-length element (first length byte 0x80). That -1 is passed straight to read(length) at line 72, which does `new byte[-1]` and throws an unchecked NegativeArraySizeException, even though readInteger declares only IOException. The signature bytes fed to asn1derToConcatenatedRS come from an externally supplied ECDSA signature, so a malformed signature escapes as an unhandled runtime exception instead of the declared IOException. readLength()'s -1 branch is handled for sequences but not here; guard the negative/indefinite value (throw IOException) before calling read(length).

issues.descricao: Claims the lenient sequence parser allows malformed or trailing DER and signature malleability in verification; the parser never sees external signatures.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: readSequence loops while(length>0) subtracting child TLV lengths but never verifies sum equals declared length nor rejects trailing bytes. WHY: lets overlong sequences and trailing garbage after the two integers be accepted as valid, diverging from strict BC ASN1InputStream and enabling signature malleability in the ECDSA verify path. HOW: enforce length==0 after loop and no remaining bytes in the outer buffer.

readSequence accepts a child whose encoded size exceeds the remaining declared sequence length. For example, `30 04 02 01 01 02 01 01` is accepted as a two-integer sequence even though its children occupy six bytes rather than the declared four, so asn1derToConcatenatedRS silently converts malformed DER instead of rejecting it. Restrict child decoding to the sequence's declared content boundary and throw IOException when a child exceeds the remaining length.

Bound each child TLV to the remaining sequence length before accepting it. Currently readNext() reads from the whole input and length may become negative, which silently ends the loop successfully. For example, `30 05 02 01 01 02 01 01` is accepted as a two-integer sequence although the second INTEGER crosses the declared sequence boundary. Decode through a stream limited to the sequence content, or reject a child whose encoded size exceeds the remaining length, so malformed DER cannot be converted as a valid signature.

issues.descricao: Claims integerToBytes can silently truncate oversized INTEGER values; inputs come from local signing and always fit the component width.

comentarios.texto: Reject INTEGER values that do not fit the requested component width instead of silently dropping their high bytes. Removing a single leading sign-padding zero is valid, but this branch also truncates actual magnitude bytes: a positive value 2^256 + 1 becomes 1 when qLength is 32. Thus DER-to-concatenated conversion can return a different signature from the one supplied. Validate nonnegative values and their bit length before padding or removing sign padding.

issues.descricao: Claims createECParams/getKeyFactory throwing UnsupportedOperationException breaks EC JWK parsing in the authz client; the client does not use that path.

comentarios.texto: The newly registered client CryptoProvider does not satisfy the existing EC JWK parsing consumer: core's AbstractJWKParser calls createECParams(name) and getKeyFactory("ECDSA") to construct an EC public key, and both operations now throw UnsupportedOperationException when this provider is selected. Consequently, a standalone authz client using this provider cannot parse EC keys for ECDSA verification, even though signature conversion is implemented. Implement the JDK-backed curve-parameter and key-factory operations (mapping ECDSA to EC as needed), rather than leaving this existing consumer with an unsupported contract.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: canManage() accepts a view-only permission on all groups. WHY: inherited requireManage() uses this result in GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup, allowing a read-only administrator to create groups or move an existing subgroup to the top level. HOW: require the MANAGE scope only, matching canManage(GroupModel).

WHAT: the new collector enumerates resources with type Groups, but getOrCreateResource creates group-instance resources without setting their type. WHY: JPAResourceStore.findByType filters by the stored type, so instance VIEW_MEMBERS grants are omitted from the group restriction used by user counts and paginated user searches, producing incorrect counts and incomplete pages. HOW: ensure group-instance resources are assigned the Groups type when created and account for already-created untyped instances.

WHAT: the collector treats an authorization resource's generated ID as the underlying group ID for both permission lookup and its returned set. WHY: AdminPermissionsSchema stores the group ID in the resource name while JPAResourceStore generates a separate resource ID; hasPermission looks up by name and therefore evaluates the all-groups fallback instead, and JpaUserProvider receives IDs that do not identify group memberships. HOW: use the instance resource name for permission lookup and returned group IDs, excluding the all-groups resource from the instance set.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() must return model group IDs, as UsersResource passes this set to getUsersCount and stores it under UserModel.GROUPS for user searches. Here groupResource.getId() is the authorization resource ID, whereas AdminPermissionsSchema names the resource with the actual group ID. Passing the resource ID to hasPermission also fails the findByName lookup and evaluates the all-groups fallback instead of the specific group's permission. Consequently specific view-members/manage-members grants do not reliably expose the group's users, and counts/search filters use the wrong identifiers. Use the resource name for both evaluation and the returned set.

The new documentation says requireManageMembers checks canManageMembership, but managing members and managing membership are separate permissions (MANAGE_MEMBERS versus MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP). This misleads callers about which authorization is required. Link to canManageMembers instead.

The added @return describes a Stream, but the method returns Set<String> and implementations return a HashSet or emptySet. Document the actual collection type so callers do not infer stream semantics.

This test passes if group-side manage-membership authorization is removed entirely. Its only denial attempt is before the user-side permission is granted and uses a nonexistent group; UserResource.joinGroup checks the user's permission before reaching auth.groups().requireManageMembership(group). The successful call then grants both permissions, so it cannot distinguish correct group authorization from no group authorization. After granting MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP on users, attempt to join an existing group before granting its MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP permission and assert ForbiddenException; then grant the group permission, join, and verify the persisted membership.

The schema names each group resource with the GroupModel ID (resolveGroup), but getId() here is the authorization resource ID. hasPermission looks up its argument using findByName, so this call misses the specific group resource and falls back to all-groups permissions. Moreover, the returned set is used as UserModel.GROUPS and therefore must contain actual group IDs. Use the resource name for both the permission lookup and the returned set; otherwise specifically granted group members disappear from user searches and counts.

canManage() accepts either VIEW or MANAGE, unlike canManage(GroupModel), which correctly requires MANAGE. Consequently an all-groups VIEW grant passes the inherited requireManage() gate and can create groups, even though it is intended to allow only reading. The new test explicitly identifies group creation as requiring the manage scope but does not test the view-only case.

AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup now uses group.getId() as the authorization resource name, not its internal resource ID. This method passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission (which resolves by name) and also returns that internal ID to UsersResource, whose search/count filters require model group IDs. Consequently group-specific view-members/manage-members permissions cannot reliably yield the intended users, and counts/searches disagree with direct user permission checks. Use the resource name for both evaluation and the returned group ID.

issues.descricao: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() accepts the VIEW scope as well as MANAGE, so an admin with only view permission on all groups passes manage checks such as group creation.
issues.textoGolden: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

comentarios.texto: The no-arg canManage() returns true when the caller holds only an all-groups VIEW permission (`hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)`), whereas the per-group canManage(GroupModel) (line 79) requires MANAGE. WHAT: a caller with only the view scope on all groups is treated as having manage rights. WHY: canManage()/requireManage() gate group creation and other manage operations (e.g. GroupsResource.addGroup -> auth.groups().requireManage()), so a read-only viewer of all groups can create/manage groups — privilege escalation. HOW: drop VIEW from the scope list so canManage() only returns true for MANAGE, aligning it with canManage(GroupModel): `return hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);`

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (line 70) evaluates hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE), identical to canView() at line 52, so a caller granted only the VIEW scope on the all-groups resource is treated as a group manager. The per-group overload canManage(GroupModel) (line 79) correctly requires only MANAGE, and AdminPermissionsSchema defines MANAGE as the manage scope for GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, so the two checks disagree. requireManage() therefore succeeds for read-only administrators, letting them create/update/delete groups, add subgroups and map group roles. Drop VIEW from the scope list so canManage() checks MANAGE only.

WHAT: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() grants global manage on VIEW scope (hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)). WHY: A caller with only view-all-groups permission passes the manage check, allowing group creation/management reserved for manage. HOW: Check only MANAGE, e.g. hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE).

issues.descricao: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses the authorization resource id instead of the resource name (the group id) for both the permission check and the returned set, so per-group view-members grants are not resolved and user filtering gets wrong ids.
issues.textoGolden: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() uses authz resource IDs (groupResource.getId()) as group IDs and looks them up via findByName. WHY: Resource names equal group IDs (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId()), so findByName(resourceId) misses and the returned set contains unusable IDs, breaking user search/count filtering by group. HOW: Use groupResource.getName() like V1 does (resource.getName().substring prefix / name) for both the hasPermission lookup and the granted set.

findByType callback passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission() and granted set, but AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup defines resource name (not UUID) as groupId and hasPermission looks up via findByName(server, groupId). Use groupResource.getName() for both check and granted set, otherwise lookups miss to all-groups fallback and callers receive authz UUIDs instead of group IDs.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses groupResource.getId() for lookup and result collection, but V2 group resources are named with the group ID (resolveGroup returns group.getId()) and hasPermission does findByName. Use groupResource.getName() in both places to evaluate the correct per-group resource and to return actual group IDs.

issues.descricao: Per-group resources are created without the Groups type, so getGroupIdsWithViewPermission's findByType never sees specific group grants.

comentarios.texto: findByType(GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE) does not enumerate the specific group resources created by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource, because that method creates them without setting their type. Consequently, specific VIEW_MEMBERS or MANAGE_MEMBERS grants are omitted from the group IDs used for user counts and database filtering. Assign the Groups type to specific group resources and ensure the all-Groups resource is not treated as a model group.

issues.descricao: The user search filter still requires legacy 'group.resource.<id>' resources, so with V2 group permissions the members of authorized groups are excluded from user searches.

comentarios.texto: The new V2 group permission IDs are passed into a JPA filter that still requires a legacy group.resource.<groupId> authorization resource. JpaUserProvider.groupsWithPermissionsSubquery checks for that prefixed name, whereas AdminPermissionsSchema creates V2 group resources named only with the group ID, so authorized group members are excluded from user searches even with valid group IDs. Update the database filtering path to support V2 resource naming rather than requiring a legacy V1 resource.

issues.descricao: The new Javadoc for requireManageMembers points to canManageMembership instead of canManageMembers.

comentarios.texto: The javadoc for requireManageMembers says it throws ForbiddenException if canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false, but this method is the require-variant of canManageMembers, not canManageMembership. The text was copied from requireManageMembership above it. It should reference canManageMembers so the documented contract matches the method name and behavior.

The Javadoc for requireManageMembers says it throws if canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false. It should refer to canManageMembers(GroupModel), which is a different check, so the doc misdescribes the method.

Javadoc for requireManageMembers references canManageMembership instead of canManageMembers (copy-paste). Fix link to {@link #canManageMembers(GroupModel)} so the contract describes the method it guards.

issues.descricao: The Javadoc of getGroupIdsWithViewPermission says it returns a Stream though the method returns a Set.

comentarios.texto: The Javadoc for getGroupIdsWithViewPermission says it returns a 'Stream of IDs', but the method returns Set<String>. Change the @return text to describe a Set of group IDs.
@return says 'Stream of IDs' but method returns Set<String> getGroupIdsWithViewPermission. Fix doc to 'Set of IDs' to match the signature.

The new @return documentation promises a Stream of IDs, but the method declares Set<String> and both implementations return sets. Describe a set of IDs instead, so the documented return contract matches what callers actually receive.

issues.descricao: Claims removing the canView filter from searchForUser lets admins see users they are not allowed to view.

comentarios.texto: The per-user `.filter(usersEvaluator::canView)` was removed from searchForUser. When the caller lacks global view and has no group-based view permission, GROUPS is not set and the search is unrestricted. Admins with only QUERY_USERS or per-user VIEW permissions can then receive user representations they are not allowed to see. Restore the `canView(user)` filter on the result stream, or return an empty stream when the caller cannot view and has no granted groups.

searchForUser() dropped the stream.users()... filter(usersEvaluator::canView) that this PR removed. Visibility is now restricted only by the session UserModel.GROUPS attribute derived from getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(), which is empty whenever the caller's view grant is a direct user-level FGAP policy rather than group membership. In that case the search query is unrestricted and the removed predicate no longer culls the rows, so the users search/count endpoints can return users the caller is not permitted to view. Restore a per-user canView filter on the stream (or otherwise ensure the query is filtered for non-group grants) when the caller lacks global view.

issues.descricao: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission scans group resources and evaluates permissions for each on every user search or count request.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() runs a full findByType scan with a per-resource evaluatePermission call for every user list/count. WHY: User searches and counts call this on each request, so cost grows O(N) with group count (N policy evaluations per request). HOW: Cache the result per request or evaluate via a single bulk permission query instead of per-resource evaluation.

issues.descricao: Claims deleting a group under V2 triggers the removal listener, which calls GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled and throws UnsupportedOperationException.

comentarios.texto: GroupPermissionsV2 is now returned by the new MgmtPermissionsV2.groups() override, but its setPermissionsEnabled(GroupModel, boolean) throws UnsupportedOperationException. The fgap removal listener (AdminPermissions.registerListener, which this PR re-registers under the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature flag) still calls management(session, realm).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false) from its group-removed handler. When the feature is enabled and a realm uses the admin-permissions (V2) client, deleting a group dispatches that event and this method raises an unhandled UnsupportedOperationException, breaking group removal. Previously groups() resolved to the V1 GroupPermissions, which does not throw. Either make setPermissionsEnabled a no-op in V2 (V2 has no per-group permission resources to disable) or stop the listener from invoking it when the V2 admin-permissions client is in use.

issues.descricao: Claims testManageGroupMembership never exercises the group-level manage-membership permission.

comentarios.texto: testManageGroupMembership does not verify the behaviour it names. It grants both an all-users MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP permission (line 295) and a group-level MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP permission on topGroup (line 298), then performs membership via UserResource.joinGroup, which authorizes through the user-scoped manage-group-membership path. The group-level MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP grant therefore never gates the successful join, and the final joinGroup(bob, topGroup) has no assertion confirming bob actually became a member. The test would still pass if group-level manage-membership evaluation were broken. Make the positive step exercise/verify the group-level permission (or assert the resulting membership list) so the claimed behaviour is actually falsified on regression.

sugestoes.texto: This new test verifies only the diagnostic text. CLIResult.assertError only checks stderr, so replacing `picocli.exit(CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED)` with a successful exit while retaining the diagnostic would still pass. The disabled-feature status is a new public command outcome in this PR; assert that `cliResult.exitCode()` equals `CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED` (4) as well so callers cannot silently receive success when the command was refused.

issues.descricao: testFeatureNotEnabled only covers the metadata subcommand, so the feature guard in the check subcommand is untested.

comentarios.texto: testFeatureNotEnabled only launches the `metadata` subcommand and never the `check` subcommand. Removing the feature guard from UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run() would therefore not fail any test. It also doesn't assert the exit code (FEATURE_DISABLED=4). Add a case for `check` and assert the exit code on both.

WHAT: testFeatureNotEnabled only exercises the metadata subcommand disabled path and never the check subcommand. WHY: the feature gate in UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run can be removed or broken without failing any test since no assertion covers its disabled message/exit code. HOW: also launch/assert the check command without --features (e.g. parameterize over metadata and check subcommands or add a second Launch).

testFeatureNotEnabled only exercises the metadata subcommand, leaving the identical ROLLING_UPDATES gate in UpdateCompatibilityCheck unverified. If the Check gate were removed, the suite still passes. Parameterize/add a second @Launch for {UpdateCompatibility.NAME, UpdateCompatibilityCheck.NAME} (with required --file or not) asserting the disabled message and FEATURE_DISABLED exit code.

issues.descricao: The disabled-feature test checks only the error message, not that the command exits with FEATURE_DISABLED (4).

comentarios.texto: The new disabled-feature test only verifies the error text, not the failure exit status. If the metadata command still prints this diagnostic but exits with 0 (or another incorrect code) instead of FEATURE_DISABLED (4), this test would still pass. Assert that cliResult.exitCode() equals CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED so the test actually protects the new disabled-feature failure contract.

issues.descricao: Claims the rolling-updates feature is not enabled for the null update strategy in UpgradeTest, so that case tests the operator without the gated feature.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: the new FeatureSpec/ROLLING_UPDATES enabling is placed after the pre-existing `if (updateStrategy == null) return kc;` early return, so for the null strategy the feature is never enabled. WHY: testCacheMaxCount(null) asserts eventuallyRollingUpgradeStatus and the PR docs state the operator requires the rolling-updates feature; the null-strategy parameter therefore exercises the operator WITHOUT the feature this PR gates on, so either the test passes for the wrong reason (feature gate ineffective) or it silently does not cover the gated path — the enablement should apply to every parameter that exercises update strategies. HOW: move the feature-enable block above the `updateStrategy == null` return (or set FeatureSpec whenever an update strategy behavior is asserted).

issues.descricao: Claims RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE changed from 4 to 3 and 4 now means feature disabled, a breaking change that needs release notes.
issues.textoGolden: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

comentarios.texto: WHAT: RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE is changed from 4 to 3 and the value 4 is reassigned to the new FEATURE_DISABLED constant. WHY: the exit code returned by the `update-compatibility check` command for a required recreate is an observable, explicitly-scriptable interface (the guide tells consumers to rely only on the exit code), so any automation keyed on the previously emitted value 4 will no longer detect the recreate case and could proceed with an unsafe rolling upgrade; exit code 4 silently changes meaning from 'recreate needed' to 'feature disabled'. HOW: if 3/4 are both free, keep RECREATE stable and use a distinct unused code for FEATURE_DISABLED; at minimum update the doc table so the reassignment is intentional and externally documented (the adoc context line shows 3 was already documented, so confirm old emitted behavior vs docs before shipping).

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE was changed from 4 to 3 and the previously-meaningful value 4 was reassigned to the new FEATURE_DISABLED outcome. The recreate exit code is a CLI output contract that external tooling/scripts key off; reusing 4 for a different result silently changes its meaning (a caller testing for 4 now treats 'feature disabled' as 'recreate required'), and recreate now returns a different code than it did before. The new feature-disabled condition should be given a fresh, unused exit code while the recreate result keeps its existing value.

issues.descricao: Claims calling picocli.exit() for the disabled-feature exit code is incorrect because it calls System.exit directly.
issues.textoGolden: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

sugestoes.texto: Successful creation in user storage leaves any previously stored local recovery-code credential intact. When a user who already has local codes regenerates them after their storage provider gains recovery-code support, UserCredentialManager.isValid falls back to RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider for inputs rejected by external storage, allowing the old local codes to authenticate despite regeneration. Remove the existing local recovery-code credential after successful external creation, preserving the replacement semantics of RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential.

The new recovery-code validator accepts a matching code without removing it from stored recovery codes. UserCredentialManager treats this external validation as final, so the local provider's consumption logic never runs; repeated logins can reuse the same recovery code indefinitely, and getCredentials recreates the full unused set each time. Persist consumption of the requested next code during successful validation and extend the integration test to reject replay and verify progression to the next code.

The new validator returns true for a matching code without updating myUser.recoveryCodes. getCredentials reconstructs the recovery model from that same unchanged list, so after a successful login the UI still requests the first code and previously accepted codes can be reused indefinitely. Consume the matched code and persist the remaining-code state on successful validation, and extend the test to perform a second login and verify that replay is rejected.

Successful validation only checks membership in the original list; it never removes the accepted code or persists consumption. getCredentials also reconstructs a fresh credential from that unchanged list on every read. Consequently, after logging out, the same recovery code can authenticate again instead of being single-use. Consume the matching code and persist the updated list as part of successful validation, with atomic synchronization so concurrent attempts cannot both accept it, and add a second-login reuse test.

The new recovery-code validator compares authentication secrets using String.equals and short-circuits with anyMatch. These operations have data-dependent execution time, exposing a timing oracle in this provider's authentication path. Compare fixed-encoding recovery-code bytes with a constant-time comparison and accumulate matches across all stored codes without early termination. This provider is test-only, so the exposure is confined to deployments running the testsuite provider.

issues.descricao: The test user-storage provider validates recovery codes without consuming the used code, so the same code can be replayed.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The new recovery-codes branch of isValid only checks whether the submitted code appears in the stored list and never removes the consumed entry. WHY: Unlike the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid (which calls removeRecoveryAuthnCode()+updateStoredCredential), the federated path never consumes a code and allCodesUsed() can never become true, so a used recovery code remains valid and can be replayed indefinitely. HOW: On a successful match, remove that entry from the stored codes (rewrite recoveryCodes.credentialData), mirroring the local provider's consume-on-success semantics.

The new recovery-code validator accepts any code in the original list without consuming the accepted code. Repeating a successful login with the same code succeeds indefinitely, while getCredentials reconstructs all original codes so the login form never advances or detects exhaustion. Validate the next unused code and persist its consumption before returning success.

The new federated recovery-code validator accepts any code in the original list but never removes a successfully used code from myUser.recoveryCodes. Consequently the same recovery code remains valid on subsequent logins, and getCredentials reconstructs the full original set every time. Consume and persist the successfully validated code (and test a second login/replay), so federated recovery codes retain their one-time semantics.

issues.descricao: getCredentials rebuilds the recovery-codes credential without copying the stored credential id, so the returned federated credential has a null id and cannot be targeted by id-based removal.
issues.textoGolden: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: getCredentials builds the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel via createFromValues but never sets its id from the stored myUser.recoveryCodes.getId() (createFromValues does not populate id). WHY: The returned federated model has a null id, so callers that identify/delete the credential by id — e.g. RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()) when all codes are used, or federated-credential deletion via getFederatedCredentialsStream — cannot target the actual credential. HOW: call model.setId(myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()) after createFromValues.

getCredentials rebuilds the recovery-code model without copying the ID assigned during updateCredential. createFromValues does not assign an ID, so the exposed federated credential has a null ID and CredentialDeleteHelper cannot resolve it by the stored credential ID for account deletion. Copy myUser.recoveryCodes.getId() to the reconstructed model before returning it.

The CredentialModel returned from getCredentials for recovery codes is built with createFromValues and never gets the stored credential's id (myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()). RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator later calls removeStoredCredentialById(model.getId()) once all codes are used, and this would pass a null id. Fix: call model.setId(myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()) after creating the model.
